query.original_query: interpretable features symbolic regression equation discovery generative model steering scientific law

sub_queries.semantic_query: interpretable features in neural networks, symbolic regression for equation discovery, generative model steering via feature dictionary learning and circuit discovery
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the intersection of interpretable feature discovery and generative model steering through the lens of sparse autoencoders and circuit analysis. Our analysis applies dictionary learning to the residual stream of a vision-language model, extracting monosemantic features that activate in response to specific visual and textual concepts. We then examine how these sparse features can be used for symbolic regression, identifying compact mathematical expressions that approximate feature activation patterns across diverse inputs. By performing causal tracing and activation patching on the identified circuits, we localize the influence of individual features within attention heads and MLP layers. Results show that steering these features via targeted interventions in the cross-attention layers of a diffusion model enables controlled modification of generated image attributes without degrading overall coherence. Our findings suggest that combining feature dictionary learning with circuit discovery provides a principled approach for linking interpretable neural representations to generative model behavior, offering a pathway toward more transparent and controllable text-to-image synthesis.

sub_queries.semantic_query: symbolic regression for equation discovery from scientific data, interpretable machine learning for scientific law discovery, generative models for scientific hypothesis generation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the capacity of symbolic regression to recover governing equations from noisy, sparse scientific datasets, comparing genetic programming-based approaches with neural-guided search strategies. Using benchmark problems from physics and biology, we measured reconstruction accuracy and parsimony of discovered expressions under varying noise levels and sample sizes. Results indicate that neural-guided methods achieve higher success rates in recovering known functional forms, particularly when data are limited, while genetic programming yields more interpretable expressions with fewer extraneous terms. We further test the hypothesis that incorporating domain-specific constraints—such as dimensional consistency and symmetry priors—improves both convergence speed and out-of-sample predictive fidelity. Findings support the view that symbolic regression, when combined with generative model-based hypothesis space exploration, can serve as a viable tool for automated scientific law discovery. However, performance degrades sharply when the underlying equation involves nested transcendental functions or when observational noise exceeds moderate thresholds, suggesting inherent limitations in current search heuristics for complex, high-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
papers.research_question: Can we find and purify polysemantic neurons? How effective is PURE in disentangling representations compared to other approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PURE, a post-hoc method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into multiple pure virtual neurons by identifying the active circuit for each feature.
papers.conclusion: PURE turns polysemantic neurons into multiple purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits, resulting in more purified features than activation-based approaches and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons exist in ResNet models and can be disentangled into pure features using circuit identification.
PURE effectively disentangles representations, leading to more interpretable virtual neurons compared to activation-based clustering.
PURE attributions are more aligned with CLIP embedding distances than activations, indicating better neuron-specific disentanglement.
PURE performs close to DINOv2 in terms of cluster separation while being computationally more efficient than DINOv2-based clustering.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on foundational models (CLIP/DINOv2) as proxies for human interpretability, which may not perfectly align with human judgment.
PURE requires a partial backward pass for each neuron, making it computationally more demanding than activation-based methods.
future_direction: Evaluation in controlled settings or using human feedback for interpretability.
Ablation studies on clustering full circuits, different attribution methods, and clustering approaches.
Investigating advantages of purified units for XAI tools like concept-based explanations, concept discovery, probing, or model correction.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to study the role of individual neurons in Deep Neural Networks. Single neurons, however, have the capability to act polysemantically and encode for multiple (unrelated) features, which renders their interpretation difficult. We present a method for disentangling polysemanticity of any Deep Neural Network by decomposing a polysemantic neuron into multiple monosemantic "virtual" neurons. This is achieved by identifying the relevant sub-graph ("circuit") for each "pure" feature. We demonstrate how our approach allows us to find and disentangle various polysemantic units of ResNet models trained on ImageNet. While evaluating feature visualizations using CLIP, our method effectively disentangles representations, improving upon methods based on neuron activations. Our code is available at https://github.com/maxdreyer/PURE.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How can we combine deep learning and symbolic regression to extract interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, specifically Graph Neural Networks, to discover physical laws and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that combines deep learning (specifically Graph Neural Networks with strong inductive biases) and symbolic regression to distill interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, enabling the discovery of physical laws and improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully distills symbolic, interpretable models from Graph Neural Networks, recovers known physical laws, discovers new formulas in cosmology, and improves generalization, offering a promising direction for interpreting deep learning models and advancing scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract known physical equations (e.g., force laws and Hamiltonians) from the learned representations of Graph Neural Networks.
Applied to a cosmology dataset, the framework discovered a new analytic formula for predicting dark matter halo concentration from the mass distribution of nearby structures.
The extracted symbolic expressions generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the original Graph Neural Network model.
The framework demonstrates that neural networks can learn representations that are linear transformations of true physical quantities (e.g., forces) when appropriate inductive biases are applied.
The approach offers a pathway to interpret neural networks and discover novel physical principles from the representations they learn.
future_direction: Extending the framework to gridded PDE data using existing symbolic regression packages for PDEs.
Using other symbolic regression packages (e.g., PySR, grammar-based methods) as drop-in replacements for eureqa in the framework.
papers.abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example-a detailed dark matter simulation-and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

papers.title: Circuit Insights: Towards Interpretability Beyond Activations
papers.research_question: How can we move beyond activation-based interpretability by using weight-based and circuit-based analysis to understand model computations, removing dependence on explainer LLMs and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods for automated interpretability that go beyond activation analysis by using model weights and circuit-level dynamics, reducing dependence on external LLMs and datasets.
papers.conclusion: WeightLens and CircuitLens advance automated interpretability by moving beyond activations, providing more robust and scalable circuit analysis while maintaining efficiency and quality.
papers.key_findings:
WeightLens matches or exceeds activation-based methods for token-based features without needing explainer LLMs or datasets.
CircuitLens captures context-dependent features and circuit-level dynamics that activation-only methods miss.
Combining weight-based and circuit-based information improves robustness and handles polysemanticity through clustering.
Interpretability of features varies with layer depth, with early and late layers being more interpretable than middle layers.
Faithfulness scores are low across methods, suggesting individual feature interventions may not strongly affect outputs due to model redundancy.
papers.limitation:
Faithfulness is low across layers and methods, likely due to model redundancy; evaluating interventions on groups of features or entire circuits might be more trustworthy.
The validation step in WeightLens does not always succeed, as some weight-based connections are meaningful only in context and cannot be validated with single-token forward passes.
future_direction: Modifying the faithfulness metric to evaluate interventions on groups of features or entire circuits.
Exploring evaluation-guided refinement of clustering parameters and results in CircuitLens.
papers.abstract: The fields of explainable AI and mechanistic interpretability aim to uncover the internal structure of neural networks, with circuit discovery as a central tool for understanding model computations. Existing approaches, however, rely on manual inspection and remain limited to toy tasks. Automated interpretability offers scalability by analyzing isolated features and their activations, but it often misses interactions between features and depends strongly on external LLMs and dataset quality. Transcoders have recently made it possible to separate feature attributions into input-dependent and input-invariant components, providing a foundation for more systematic circuit analysis. Building on this, we propose WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods that go beyond activation-based analysis. WeightLens interprets features directly from their learned weights, removing the need for explainer models or datasets while matching or exceeding the performance of existing methods on context-independent features. CircuitLens captures how feature activations arise from interactions between components, revealing circuit-level dynamics that activation-only approaches cannot identify. Together, these methods increase interpretability robustness and enhance scalable mechanistic analysis of circuits while maintaining efficiency and quality.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we find interpretable features in large language models by decomposing MLP activations using semi-nonnegative matrix factorization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNMF for decomposing MLP activations into interpretable features, outperforming SAEs and supervised baselines in causal steering, and reveals hierarchical structure in MLP activation space.
papers.conclusion: SNMF is a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SNMF-derived features outperform SAEs and a supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering.
SNMF features align with human-interpretable concepts and show good concept detection.
Recursive SNMF reveals hierarchical merging of features, e.g., fine-grained concepts into high-level ones.
Specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features.
MLP features are compositional and exhibit a parts-based decomposition.
papers.limitation: A minority of MLP features receive negative scores, indicating they respond more strongly to neutral contexts, possibly reflecting sensitivity to noise or layer-specific biases.
future_direction: Optimizations for SNMF initialization and training
papers.abstract: A central goal for mechanistic interpretability has been to identify the right units of analysis in large language models (LLMs) that causally explain their outputs. While early work focused on individual neurons, evidence that neurons often encode multiple concepts has motivated a shift toward analyzing directions in activation space. A key question is how to find directions that capture interpretable features in an unsupervised manner. Current methods rely on dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), commonly trained over residual stream activations to learn directions from scratch. However, SAEs often struggle in causal evaluations and lack intrinsic interpretability, as their learning is not explicitly tied to the computations of the model. Here, we tackle these limitations by directly decomposing MLP activations with semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF), such that the learned features are (a) sparse linear combinations of co-activated neurons, and (b) mapped to their activating inputs, making them directly interpretable. Experiments on Llama 3.1, Gemma 2 and GPT-2 show that SNMF derived features outperform SAEs and a strong supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering, while aligning with human-interpretable concepts. Further analysis reveals that specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features, exposing a hierarchical structure in the MLP's activation space. Together, these results position SNMF as a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
papers.research_question: How to leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformer language models without linear approximations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using Sparse Autoencoders and Transcoders to refactor Transformer computation into a linear graph, enabling fine-grained circuit discovery without approximation via Hierarchical Attribution.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformers, revealing detailed and beautiful internal structures that were previously obscured by coarser analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
The pipeline identifies fine-grained circuits for bracket matching, induction, and Indirect Object Identification (IOI) in GPT-2 Small.
SAE-based circuits reveal more detailed structural information than coarser head-level circuit analyses.
The IOI circuit differs at the feature level between two similar prompt templates (sJohn and sMary), showing nuanced mechanistic distinctions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to certain inputs and might not generalize to other settings.
future_direction: Extending the method to extract more general circuits for abstract behaviors.
papers.abstract: Circuit analysis of any certain model behavior is a central task in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce our circuit discovery pipeline with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant called Transcoders. With these two modules inserted into the model, the model's computation graph with respect to OV and MLP circuits becomes strictly linear. Our methods do not require linear approximation to compute the causal effect of each node. This fine-grained graph identifies both end-to-end and local circuits accounting for either logits or intermediate features. We can scalably apply this pipeline with a technique called Hierarchical Attribution. We analyze three kinds of circuits in GPT-2 Small: bracket, induction, and Indirect Object Identification circuits. Our results reveal new findings underlying existing discoveries.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Towards Combinatorial Interpretability of Neural Computation
papers.research_question: Does a neural network trained via gradient descent learn to use feature channel coding, a combinatorial coding scheme for computing Boolean expressions? How can this coding be used to interpret neural computation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces combinatorial interpretability and the feature channel coding hypothesis, showing that neural networks learn to use feature channel coding for Boolean functions and providing a method to extract these codes directly from weight matrices.
papers.conclusion: Combinatorial interpretability via feature channel coding provides a powerful method for understanding neural computation, at least for Boolean functions, and offers a basis for interpreting both artificial and biological neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained on Boolean functions learn to use feature channel coding.
Feature channel coding can be extracted combinatorially from the weight matrices without examining activations or training auxiliary models.
The combinatorial approach explains scaling laws: there is a combinatorial limit to the number of features that can be coded given the network size, leading to representational collapse.
Coding patterns emerge dynamically during gradient descent training, structuring weights from initial randomness.
The approach can be extended to deeper networks via a framework of cascading feature disentanglement, though this is preliminary.
papers.limitation:
The current study is restricted to Boolean functions and small networks.
The method for deeper networks (cascading feature disentanglement) is preliminary and not fully algorithmic.
future_direction: Extending the combinatorial approach to deeper and larger real-world networks.
Applying the framework to understand sparsity, quantization, and the linear representation hypothesis.
Investigating the extent to which real production neural networks contain Boolean features and their codes.
papers.abstract: We introduce combinatorial interpretability, a methodology for understanding neural computation by analyzing the combinatorial structures in the sign-based categorization of a network's weights and biases. We demonstrate its power through feature channel coding, a theory that explains how neural networks compute Boolean expressions and potentially underlies other categories of neural network computation. According to this theory, features are computed via feature channels: unique cross-neuron encodings shared among the inputs the feature operates on. Because different feature channels share neurons, the neurons are polysemantic and the channels interfere with one another, making the computation appear inscrutable. We show how to decipher these computations by analyzing a network's feature channel coding, offering complete mechanistic interpretations of several small neural networks that were trained with gradient descent. Crucially, this is achieved via static combinatorial analysis of the weight matrices, without examining activations or training new autoencoding networks. Feature channel coding reframes the superposition hypothesis, shifting the focus from neuron activation directionality in high-dimensional space to the combinatorial structure of codes. It also allows us for the first time to exactly quantify and explain the relationship between a network's parameter size and its computational capacity (i.e. the set of features it can compute with low error), a relationship that is implicitly at the core of many modern scaling laws. Though our initial studies of feature channel coding are restricted to Boolean functions, we believe they provide a rich, controlled, and informative research space, and that the path we propose for combinatorial interpretation of neural computation can provide a basis for understanding both artificial and biological neural circuits.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Closed-Form Interpretation of Neural Network Latent Spaces with Symbolic Gradients
papers.research_question: How can we extract closed-form symbolic interpretations of neurons in neural network latent spaces without prior knowledge of the concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for closed-form interpretation of neurons in neural network latent spaces by matching normalized gradients with symbolic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Developed a framework to interpret any single neuron in neural network latent spaces as a symbolic equation, enabling scientific discovery from latent space models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully retrieves ground truth symbolic expressions for matrix invariants and conserved quantities from Siamese network latent neurons.
The method outperforms direct symbolic regression when the latent encoding is non-linear.
The symbolic search sometimes finds approximate expressions that are mathematically equivalent or Taylor expansions of the ground truth.
The framework is the first general method for extracting concepts from latent spaces in closed form.
papers.limitation: The approach is limited by the expressibility of symbolic search algorithms and the challenge of isolating single neurons through bottlenecks or disentanglement.
papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that artificial neural networks like autoencoders or Siamese networks encode meaningful concepts in their latent spaces. However, there does not exist a comprehensive framework for retrieving this information in a human-readable form without prior knowledge. In quantitative disciplines concepts are typically formulated as equations. Hence, in order to extract these concepts, we introduce a framework for finding closed-form interpretations of neurons in latent spaces of artificial neural networks. The interpretation framework is based on embedding trained neural networks into an equivalence class of functions that encode the same concept. We interpret these neural networks by finding an intersection between the equivalence class and human-readable equations defined by a symbolic search space. Computationally, this framework is based on finding a symbolic expression whose normalized gradients match the normalized gradients of a specific neuron with respect to the input variables. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by retrieving invariants of matrices and conserved quantities of dynamical systems from latent spaces of Siamese neural networks.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Decomposing Language Models Into Understandable Components
papers.research_question: How can we decompose language models into interpretable components to understand their behavior, moving beyond individual neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using dictionary learning to decompose language models into interpretable features, which are more understandable than individual neurons and enable targeted steering of model behavior.
papers.conclusion: This decomposition method moves past the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons, potentially enabling monitoring and steering of model behavior for improved safety and reliability. The next challenge is scaling the approach to larger frontier models.
papers.key_findings:
Features are significantly more interpretable than neurons, as validated by blinded human evaluator scores.
Features allow for targeted steering of model behavior, causing predictable changes when artificially activated.
The learned features are largely universal between different models.
Varying the number of features provides a control for the resolution of model interpretation, from coarse to refined views.
This approach overcomes the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons in mechanistic understanding.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on a small model and scaling to larger frontier models is an engineering obstacle.
future_direction: Scaling the approach up to frontier models which are larger and more complicated.
