papers.abstract: How can we decompose language models into interpretable components to understand their behavior, moving beyond individual neurons? Introduces a method using dictionary learning to decompose language models into interpretable features, which are more understandable than individual neurons and enable targeted steering of model behavior. This decomposition method moves past the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons, potentially enabling monitoring and steering of model behavior for improved safety and reliability. The next challenge is scaling the approach to larger frontier models.

papers.title: Attacking Superposition with Dictionary Learning Features as The Simplest Factorization Dictionary Learning Worries Fractional Dimensionality and Pressure The Two Circle Phenomenon in Memorization Weight Superposition Attention Head Superposition Feature Manifold Toy Model
papers.research_question: How can dictionary learning be used to extract features from superposition in neural networks, and what are the challenges and insights from toy models?
papers.core_contribution: The blog presents developing ideas on using dictionary learning to attack superposition in neural networks, with conceptual contributions on feature factorization, geometry, and challenges in extracting interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: These are preliminary research notes sharing ongoing work on superposition and dictionary learning, with the aim of building infrastructure for larger-scale investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary learning solutions 'bounce' when the dictionary size matches the true number of features in synthetic data, as shown by plotting Mean Squared Error vs Total Information.
Dictionary learning may be too strong for neural networks due to concerns like compressed sensing allowing arbitrary functions and non-zero-centered representations.
Feature pressure and training duration affect the geometry of superposition in toy models, leading to uniform polyhedra or other structures.
Attention heads can implement skip-trigram circuits in superposition, meaning circuits can be distributed across multiple heads, cautioning against studying heads in isolation.
Feature manifolds in toy models show emergent discretization, where continuous manifolds are represented by discrete neurons, similar to value coding in neuroscience.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be too strong for neural networks because compressed sensing algorithms allow arbitrary functions, which might not align with how networks cheaply retrieve features.
The representation may not be zero-centered, which typical dictionary learning algorithms do not handle well.
The smallest length scale discretization in feature manifold toy models may be an optimization failure.
future_direction: Systematic, large-scale investigation of superposition in real models using dictionary learning.
Additional research to understand the emergent discretization in feature manifolds.
papers.abstract: How can dictionary learning be used to extract features from superposition in neural networks, and what are the challenges and insights from toy models? The blog presents developing ideas on using dictionary learning to attack superposition in neural networks, with conceptual contributions on feature factorization, geometry, and challenges in extracting interpretable features. These are preliminary research notes sharing ongoing work on superposition and dictionary learning, with the aim of building infrastructure for larger-scale investigations.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Visual Features in Artificial and Biological Neural Systems
papers.research_question: Does the activation space of neural networks contain meaningful, interpretable directions that are not aligned with individual neurons? And does this also apply to biological neural systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated method for quantifying visual interpretability using an interpretability index (II) and shows that non-axis aligned directions in activation space, found via methods like K-Means, are more interpretable than individual neurons, with similar findings in biological neural data.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that meaningful, interpretable directions exist in activation space beyond individual neurons in both artificial and biological neural systems, supporting the superposition hypothesis and suggesting universal coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpretability index (II) based on LPIPS similarity correlates with human psychophysics judgments, especially in early layers.
K-Means clusters in activation space yield directions that are more interpretable than individual neurons across low, mid, and high-level semantics.
Pairwise synergies between neurons can produce more interpretable directions, with correlated neurons tending to have higher synergy.
In biological neural data (macaque IT cortex and human fMRI), similar patterns are found, suggesting superposition might be deployed by the brain.
Interpretable directions transfer better across subjects and recording sessions than individual units, indicating greater universality.
papers.limitation: The interpretability metric based on LPIPS matches human judgments well for early layers but has room for improvement, particularly for later layers.
papers.abstract: Single neurons in neural networks are often interpretable in that they represent individual, intuitively meaningful features. However, many neurons exhibit $\textit{mixed selectivity}$, i.e., they represent multiple unrelated features. A recent hypothesis proposes that features in deep networks may be represented in $\textit{superposition}$, i.e., on non-orthogonal axes by multiple neurons, since the number of possible interpretable features in natural data is generally larger than the number of neurons in a given network. Accordingly, we should be able to find meaningful directions in activation space that are not aligned with individual neurons. Here, we propose (1) an automated method for quantifying visual interpretability that is validated against a large database of human psychophysics judgments of neuron interpretability, and (2) an approach for finding meaningful directions in network activation space. We leverage these methods to discover directions in convolutional neural networks that are more intuitively meaningful than individual neurons, as we confirm and investigate in a series of analyses. Moreover, we apply the same method to three recent datasets of visual neural responses in the brain and find that our conclusions largely transfer to real neural data, suggesting that superposition might be deployed by the brain. This also provides a link with disentanglement and raises fundamental questions about robust, efficient and factorized representations in both artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: Insights on Galaxy Evolution from Interpretable Sparse Feature Networks
papers.research_question: How can we make deep neural networks interpretable for galaxy image analysis to learn the relationship between pixel-level features and galaxy properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Feature Network (SFNet), a CNN with a top-k sparsity constraint that produces interpretable features for predicting galaxy properties without sacrificing accuracy.
papers.conclusion: SFNet provides interpretable features for galaxy property prediction, advancing explainable deep learning in the physical sciences without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
SFNet achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on predicting galaxy properties like emission line fluxes and gas-phase metallicity.
The learned sparse features correspond to physically interpretable galaxy morphologies (e.g., red ellipticals, blue edge-on disks).
SFNet features are more robust for linear prediction than principal components extracted from a regular CNN.
SFNet features are distinct from those learned by a standard CNN trained on morphological classifications (Zoobot).
SFNet enables simple linear equations that relate galaxy properties to interpretable image features.
papers.limitation:
Galaxy evolution involves complex physical processes not always imprinted in galaxy morphology, limiting the physics that can be learned from images alone.
The optimization procedure and hyperparameters have not been comprehensively varied.
future_direction: Explore additional sparsity constraints such as decorrelation layers or regularization terms.
Use a CNN architecture with a smaller receptive field to enhance feature localization.
Deploy activation maximization to further hone in on activating features.
papers.abstract: Galaxy appearances reveal the physics of how they formed and evolved. Machine learning models can now exploit galaxies' information-rich morphologies to predict physical properties directly from image cutouts. Learning the relationship between pixel-level features and galaxy properties is essential for building a physical understanding of galaxy evolution, but we are still unable to explicate the details of how deep neural networks represent image features. To address this lack of interpretability, we present a novel neural network architecture called a Sparse Feature Network (SFNet). SFNets produce interpretable features that can be linearly combined in order to estimate galaxy properties like optical emission line ratios or gas-phase metallicity. We find that SFNets do not sacrifice accuracy in order to gain interpretability, and that they perform comparably well to cutting-edge models on astronomical machine learning tasks. Our novel approach is valuable for finding physical patterns in large datasets and helping astronomers interpret machine learning results.

papers.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
papers.research_question: Does training weight-sparse transformers lead to more interpretable circuits? How does sparsity trade off with capability and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Training weight-sparse transformers leads to interpretable circuits with neurons and residual channels corresponding to natural concepts. Sparsity trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves this trade-off.
papers.conclusion: Weight-sparse transformers enable the discovery of highly interpretable circuits, validated by rigorous ablation, though scaling sparse models remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-sparse models yield circuits that are roughly 16-fold smaller than dense models of comparable pretraining loss.
Circuits in sparse models are necessary and sufficient for task performance, as shown by ablation studies.
Scaling total parameter count improves the capability-interpretability Pareto frontier.
Qualitative analysis reveals interpretable algorithms for tasks like string closing, bracket counting, and variable type tracking.
Preliminary results show that bridges can be used to extract circuits from existing dense models.
papers.limitation:
Scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge.
Sparse models are extremely inefficient to train and deploy, and are unlikely to ever reach frontier capabilities.
The use of mean ablation for circuit validation is a weaker form of faithfulness compared to full causal scrubbing.
future_direction: Pushing circuit faithfulness to full causal scrubbing and beyond.
Scaling up sparse models with systems optimizations.
Applying the bridge method more extensively to explain existing dense models.
papers.abstract: Finding human-understandable circuits in language models is a central goal of the field of mechanistic interpretability. We train models to have more understandable circuits by constraining most of their weights to be zeros, so that each neuron only has a few connections. To recover fine-grained circuits underlying each of several hand-crafted tasks, we prune the models to isolate the part responsible for the task. These circuits often contain neurons and residual channels that correspond to natural concepts, with a small number of straightforwardly interpretable connections between them. We study how these models scale and find that making weights sparser trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves the capability-interpretability frontier. However, scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge. In addition to training weight-sparse models de novo, we show preliminary results suggesting our method can also be adapted to explain existing dense models. Our work produces circuits that achieve an unprecedented level of human understandability and validates them with considerable rigor.

papers.title: Improving Neuron-level Interpretability with White-box Language Models
papers.research_question: Can building sparsity directly into the language model architecture (via a white-box design) improve neuron-level interpretability compared to post-hoc methods like sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a white-box transformer-like architecture (crate) that embeds sparse coding directly into the model, leading to significantly improved neuron-level interpretability compared to standard transformers like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Replacing the standard transformer architecture with the white-box crate model significantly improves neuron-level interpretability, pointing towards a promising direction for building more interpretable foundation models with built-in sparse coding.
papers.key_findings:
crate achieves up to 103% relative improvement in neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2 across multiple evaluation metrics.
The improved interpretability is steady across different layers and model sizes.
crate's interpretability stems from its ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens.
crate has more optimal representations for interpretability than GPT-2, as applying sparse autoencoders (SAE) to crate yields smaller improvements than applying SAE to GPT-2.
crate can be steered without the reconstruction loss inherent in post-hoc SAE methods.
papers.limitation: The performance of crate on the next-token prediction task is not as good as GPT-2, potentially due to the introduction of sparsity.
future_direction: Investigate a better trade-off between performance and interpretability in language models with built-in sparsity.
Research more qualitative mechanisms in white-box language models and how to use them for downstream edits.
papers.abstract: Neurons in auto-regressive language models like GPT-2 can be interpreted by analyzing their activation patterns. Recent studies have shown that techniques such as dictionary learning, a form of post-hoc sparse coding, enhance this neuron-level interpretability. In our research, we are driven by the goal to fundamentally improve neural network interpretability by embedding sparse coding directly within the model architecture, rather than applying it as an afterthought. In our study, we introduce a white-box transformer-like architecture named Coding RAte TransformEr (CRATE), explicitly engineered to capture sparse, low-dimensional structures within data distributions. Our comprehensive experiments showcase significant improvements (up to 103% relative improvement) in neuron-level interpretability across a variety of evaluation metrics. Detailed investigations confirm that this enhanced interpretability is steady across different layers irrespective of the model size, underlining CRATE's robust performance in enhancing neural network interpretability. Further analysis shows that CRATE's increased interpretability comes from its enhanced ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens. These findings point towards a promising direction for creating white-box foundation models that excel in neuron-level interpretation.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: GINN-KAN: Interpretability pipelining with applications in Physics Informed Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we create an interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN to overcome their individual limitations and be effectively applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GINN-KAN, a novel interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN, and demonstrates its application to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), creating interpretable PINNs that outperform black-box networks.
papers.conclusion: GINN-KAN represents a significant step forward in developing interpretable neural networks, offering a promising balance between interpretability and performance, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets.
GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform traditional PINNs with black-box networks on 15 different partial differential equations.
GINN struggles to learn non-Laurent polynomial (non-LP) equations, while KAN struggles to learn equations containing multiplicative terms.
GINN-KAN combines the strengths of both GINN and KAN, performing well on both LP and non-LP equations and on equations with multiplications.
GINN-KAN can be trained using backpropagation and integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal adjustments.
papers.limitation: GINN-KAN is restricted to inputs with positive values, a limitation inherited from GINN.
future_direction: Explore more robust architectures that maintain interpretability while overcoming the positive input limitation.
Develop better regularization techniques to enable GINN-KAN to accurately discover concise ground truth equations.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful function approximators, yet their ``black-box" nature often renders them opaque and difficult to interpret. While many post-hoc explanation methods exist, they typically fail to capture the underlying reasoning processes of the networks. A truly interpretable neural network would be trained similarly to conventional models using techniques such as backpropagation, but additionally provide insights into the learned input-output relationships. In this work, we introduce the concept of interpretability pipelineing, to incorporate multiple interpretability techniques to outperform each individual technique. To this end, we first evaluate several architectures that promise such interpretability, with a particular focus on two recent models selected for their potential to incorporate interpretability into standard neural network architectures while still leveraging backpropagation: the Growing Interpretable Neural Network (GINN) and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN). We analyze the limitations and strengths of each and introduce a novel interpretable neural network GINN-KAN that synthesizes the advantages of both models. When tested on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets, GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN. To highlight the capabilities and the generalizability of this approach, we position GINN-KAN as an alternative to conventional black-box networks in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). We expect this to have far-reaching implications in the application of deep learning pipelines in the natural sciences. Our experiments with this interpretable PINN on 15 different partial differential equations demonstrate that GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform PINNs with black-box networks in solving differential equations and surpass the capabilities of both GINN and KAN.

papers.title: The Interpretable Dictionary in Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: Does sparse coding under sparsity constraints yield more interpretable neural networks compared to standard deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse coding with sparsity constraints produces more interpretable neural networks than standard deep learning, as demonstrated by selective activations and lower cross-correlation in dictionary elements.
papers.conclusion: Sparse coding with elements of sparsity, competition, and selectivity leads to interpretable models where each neuron's contribution can be directly determined, unlike deep learning models where explanations are confounded by dense activations.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse coding dictionary elements are interpretable and correspond to semantic features in information graphics.
Activations in sparse coding are sparse and selective, activating only for relevant image patches, unlike CNN activations which are dense and non-specific.
Cross-correlation analysis shows that sparse coding has significantly lower mean intra- and inter-image correlation compared to CNN filters.
The sparse coding model achieves high sparsity with around 4% of elements active per image and low frequency of usage per dictionary element.
Qualitative comparisons show that sparse coding activations directly attribute image components to specific dictionary elements, enabling clear explanations.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs), specifically deep learning networks, have often been labeled as black boxes due to the fact that the internal representation of the data is not easily interpretable. In our work, we illustrate that an ANN, trained using sparse coding under specific sparsity constraints, yields a more interpretable model than the standard deep learning model. The dictionary learned by sparse coding can be more easily understood and the activations of these elements creates a selective feature output. We compare and contrast our sparse coding model with an equivalent feed forward convolutional autoencoder trained on the same data. Our results show both qualitative and quantitative benefits in the interpretation of the learned sparse coding dictionary as well as the internal activation representations.

papers.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
papers.research_question: Can MLP neurons serve as a sparse basis for circuit tracing, comparable to sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs for circuit tracing, enabling effective circuit tracing without additional training costs.
papers.conclusion: MLP neurons provide a sparse basis for circuit tracing, advancing automated interpretability without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations are a much sparser basis than MLP outputs for circuit tracing, reducing circuit size by 100x.
Using RelP attribution closes the performance gap between MLP activations and SAE features.
The findings hold even with unpaired data (without counterfactual inputs).
RelP finds more faithful edges than Integrated Gradients for circuit tracing.
In a multi-hop reasoning task, small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps and can be steered to change model output.
papers.abstract: The high-level concepts that a neural network uses to perform computation need not be aligned to individual neurons (Smolensky, 1986). Language model interpretability research has thus turned to techniques such as \textit{sparse autoencoders} (SAEs) to decompose the neuron basis into more interpretable units of model computation, for tasks such as \textit{circuit tracing}. However, not all neuron-based representations are uninterpretable. For the first time, we empirically show that \textbf{MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs}. We use this finding to develop an end-to-end pipeline for circuit tracing on the MLP neuron basis, which locates causal circuitry on a variety of tasks using gradient-based attribution. On a standard subject-verb agreement benchmark (Marks et al., 2025), a circuit of $\approx 10^2$ MLP neurons is enough to control model behaviour. On the multi-hop city $\to$ state $\to$ capital task from Lindsey et al., 2025, we find a circuit in which small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps (e.g.~`map city to its state'), and can be steered to change the model's output. This work thus advances automated interpretability of language models without additional training costs.

papers.title: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Improving Circuit Faithfulness via Better Edge Selection
papers.research_question: How to improve circuit faithfulness via better edge selection in circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes bootstrapping, positive-negative ratio (PNR), and integer linear programming (ILP) for edge selection in circuit discovery, improving faithfulness over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Principled edge selection improves faithfulness and enables more robust circuit discovery, despite computational limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Bootstrapping identifies edges with consistent attribution scores, filtering out unstable ones.
Positive-negative ratio (PNR) selection balances positive and negative edges, improving circuit faithfulness.
Integer linear programming (ILP) provides globally optimal edge selection compared to greedy algorithms.
Combinations of these methods outperform baseline approaches across multiple models and tasks on MIB metrics.
papers.limitation:
ILP optimization scales poorly with edge count, limiting applicability to larger models.
Optimal ratio of positive edges varies by models and tasks, requiring task-specific tuning.
Gap between state-of-the-art attribution methods and 'ground truth' edge importance scores limits faithfulness gains from ILP.
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges in mechanistic interpretability is circuit discovery, determining which parts of a model perform a given task. We build on the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) and propose three key improvements to circuit discovery. First, we use bootstrapping to identify edges with consistent attribution scores. Second, we introduce a simple ratio-based selection strategy to prioritize strong positive-scoring edges, balancing performance and faithfulness. Third, we replace the standard greedy selection with an integer linear programming formulation. Our methods yield more faithful circuits and outperform prior approaches across multiple MIB tasks and models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/MIB-Shared-Task.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Symbolic Synthesis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be combined with symbolic programs to improve data-efficient generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces G-SSNNs, a class of neural modules that inject features from synthesized symbolic programs to improve data efficiency and generalization.
papers.conclusion: G-SSNNs improve data efficiency and generalization on a binary prediction task over Raven's Progressive Matrices and allow derivation of symbolic program semantics without manual engineering.
papers.key_findings:
G-SSNN modules modulate the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization.
Training G-SSNNs provides information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering, which is compact and amenable to abstraction.
future_direction: Investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs.
papers.abstract: Neural networks adapt very well to distributed and continuous representations, but struggle to generalize from small amounts of data. Symbolic systems commonly achieve data efficient generalization by exploiting modularity to benefit from local and discrete features of a representation. These features allow symbolic programs to be improved one module at a time and to experience combinatorial growth in the values they can successfully process. However, it is difficult to design a component that can be used to form symbolic abstractions and which is adequately overparametrized to learn arbitrary high-dimensional transformations. I present Graph-based Symbolically Synthesized Neural Networks (G-SSNNs), a class of neural modules that operate on representations modified with synthesized symbolic programs to include a fixed set of local and discrete features. I demonstrate that the choice of injected features within a G-SSNN module modulates the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization. By training G-SSNNs, we also derive information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering. This information is compact and amenable to abstraction, but can also be flexibly recontextualized for other high-dimensional settings. In future work, I will investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs. Experimental code and data are available at https://github.com/shlomenu/symbolically_synthesized_networks .

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
One-step training is sufficient for learning meaningful features applicable to multi-step diffusion models.
papers.limitation: The change pose task is hard to achieve with the current RIEBench setup.
future_direction: Improving feature selection strategies for delete interventions
Extending SAEs to other diffusion models
Using learned features for advanced image editing and control
papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been shown to decompose intermediate representations that often are not interpretable directly into sparse sums of interpretable features, facilitating better control and subsequent analysis. However, similar analyses and approaches have been lacking for text-to-image models. We investigate the possibility of using SAEs to learn interpretable features for SDXL Turbo, a few-step text-to-image diffusion model. To this end, we train SAEs on the updates performed by transformer blocks within SDXL Turbo's denoising U-net in its 1-step setting. Interestingly, we find that they generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and even to the multi-step SDXL base model (i.e., a different model) without additional training. In addition, we show that their learned features are interpretable, causally influence the generation process, and reveal specialization among the blocks. We do so by creating RIEBench, a representation-based image editing benchmark, for editing images while they are generated by turning on and off individual SAE features. This allows us to track which transformer blocks' features are the most impactful depending on the edit category. Our work is the first investigation of SAEs for interpretability in text-to-image diffusion models and our results establish SAEs as a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image models.

papers.title: Restyling Unsupervised Concept Based Interpretable Networks with Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the visualization and interpretation of learnt unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks for large-scale images?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VisCoIN, a novel architecture for unsupervised concept-based interpretable networks that maps concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model, enabling high-quality visualization and interactive interpretation of learnt concepts.
papers.conclusion: VisCoIN effectively leverages pretrained generative models to improve visualization and interpretation of unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks, achieving high prediction performance and learning more faithful and consistent concepts.
papers.key_findings:
VisCoIN achieves comparable prediction accuracy to baseline methods while improving reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity.
The learnt concepts in VisCoIN are more faithful and consistent compared to previous unsupervised CoINs.
The visualization pipeline based on the generative model allows for granular and interactive interpretation of concepts by modifying concept activations and observing changes in generated images.
papers.limitation:
Cannot guarantee that concepts precisely correspond to human concepts and may encode additional information.
System quality is limited by the quality of the pretrained generative model.
Linear trajectories in latent space may not be optimal for latent traversals.
papers.abstract: Developing inherently interpretable models for prediction has gained prominence in recent years. A subclass of these models, wherein the interpretable network relies on learning high-level concepts, are valued because of closeness of concept representations to human communication. However, the visualization and understanding of the learnt unsupervised dictionary of concepts encounters major limitations, especially for large-scale images. We propose here a novel method that relies on mapping the concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The use of a generative model enables high quality visualization, and lays out an intuitive and interactive procedure for better interpretation of the learnt concepts by imputing concept activations and visualizing generated modifications. Furthermore, leveraging pretrained generative models has the additional advantage of making the training of the system more efficient. We quantitatively ascertain the efficacy of our method in terms of accuracy of the interpretable prediction network, fidelity of reconstruction, as well as faithfulness and consistency of learnt concepts. The experiments are conducted on multiple image recognition benchmarks for large-scale images. Project page available at https://jayneelparekh.github.io/VisCoIN_project_page/

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Can a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery techniques in identifying important subnetworks (circuits) within neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP), a method that uses a linear approximation of activation patching via gradients, outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods (like ACDC) in recovering known circuits while being significantly more computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, though running ACDC on the subnetwork found by EAP can further improve results.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) achieves higher AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is computationally efficient, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass, unlike ACDC which scales exponentially with the number of nodes.
The linear approximation used in attribution patching can be inaccurate (e.g., concave curves) and may overestimate the effect of ablating an edge.
Running ACDC on the subgraph pruned by EAP can improve circuit identification performance over using EAP alone.
Attribution scores for edges in known circuits (e.g., name movers in IOI) align with their intuitive function, validating the method's outputs.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used for interpretability (like recovery of human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding.
Human-found circuits are imperfect, which adds noise to the evaluation metric.
The linear approximation in attribution patching can be inaccurate, particularly for edges involving model embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research has recently attracted attention as a potential research direction that could scale explanations of neural network behavior to large models. Existing automated circuit discovery work applies activation patching to identify subnetworks responsible for solving specific tasks (circuits). In this work, we show that a simple method based on attribution patching outperforms all existing methods while requiring just two forward passes and a backward pass. We apply a linear approximation to activation patching to estimate the importance of each edge in the computational subgraph. Using this approximation, we prune the least important edges of the network. We survey the performance and limitations of this method, finding that averaged over all tasks our method has greater AUC from circuit recovery than other methods.

papers.title: Self-Ablating Transformers: More Interpretability, Less Sparsity
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between sparsity and interpretability in transformers? Does inducing sparsity during training via a self-ablation mechanism enhance interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-ablation mechanism that enforces selective activation (k-winner-takes-all) during training, leading to improved interpretability (more localized circuits, specialized neurons) without necessarily increasing overall sparsity.
papers.conclusion: Self-ablation improves transformer interpretability across multiple indicators (circuit localization, feature disentanglement, neuron explainability) by promoting functional specialization and localized computation, challenging the simple intuition that sparsity alone leads to interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Self-ablation reduces circuit complexity, as shown by fewer edges in ACDC circuits for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
Self-ablation leads to sparser feature representations (lower L0 norm in Sparse Autoencoders) and better reconstruction fidelity (higher CE score).
Self-ablation improves neuron explainability, with ablated models achieving higher automated explanation scores.
Self-ablation results in more focused neuron activation patterns, evidenced by lower graph density, lower transitivity, and increased specialization metrics in Neuron-to-Graph analysis.
Self-ablation incurs only a modest increase in validation perplexity, indicating a manageable trade-off between interpretability and language modeling performance.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation was conducted on the linguistically simple TinyStories dataset, which lacks complex syntax, diverse vocabulary, and abstract reasoning, limiting generalizability to real-world language.
Experiments were conducted on relatively small models; it is unknown how the self-ablation mechanism scales to much larger architectures.
future_direction: Evaluating self-ablation on linguistically diverse datasets to test scalability to complex linguistic phenomena.
Investigating the impact of model scale on the self-ablation mechanism's effects.
Exploring the application of self-ablation within a fine-tuning paradigm to improve interpretability of existing large language models.
papers.abstract: A growing intuition in machine learning suggests a link between sparsity and interpretability. We introduce a novel self-ablation mechanism to investigate this connection ante-hoc in the context of language transformers. Our approach dynamically enforces a k-winner-takes-all constraint, forcing the model to demonstrate selective activation across neuron and attention units. Unlike post-hoc methods that analyze already-trained models, our approach integrates interpretability directly into model training, promoting feature localization from inception.
