This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to improve interpretability and steerability, and how can we quantitatively evaluate the monosemanticity of neurons in such models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the MonoSemanticity score (MS) to evaluate neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), validates MS with a human study, and demonstrates that SAEs can steer multimodal LLM outputs by intervening on vision encoder neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) effectively improve neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models, with the MonoSemanticity score providing a reliable metric aligned with human judgment, and shows that SAEs enable unsupervised concept-based steering of multimodal LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs significantly increase the monosemanticity of individual neurons in VLMs compared to original neurons.
Sparsity and wider latent dimensions are the most influential factors for improving monosemanticity.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve overall superior monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAE variants.
SAE interventions on the vision encoder can steer multimodal LLM (e.g., LLaVA) outputs to insert or suppress specific concepts without modifying the language model.
The proposed MonoSemanticity score aligns well with human perception of similarity, as validated by a large-scale user study.
papers.limitation:
High MS score neurons do not always produce precise effects when used to steer MLLM outputs; for example, a 'golden retriever' neuron might trigger any dog-related output due to limited fine-grained understanding in MLLMs.
A fraction of SAE neurons that act as feature detectors do not exhibit any clear steering effect.
future_direction: Adapting the MonoSemanticity metric to text representations.
Investigating the interplay between specialized (low-level) and broad (high-level) concepts within learned representations.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently gained attention as a means to improve the interpretability and steerability of Large Language Models (LLMs), both of which are essential for AI safety. In this work, we extend the application of SAEs to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, and introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating monosemanticity at the neuron-level in visual representations. To ensure that our evaluation aligns with human perception, we propose a benchmark derived from a large-scale user study. Our experimental results reveal that SAEs trained on VLMs significantly enhance the monosemanticity of individual neurons, with sparsity and wide latents being the most influential factors. Further, we demonstrate that applying SAE interventions on CLIP's vision encoder directly steers multimodal LLM outputs (e.g., LLaVA), without any modifications to the underlying language model. These findings emphasize the practicality and efficacy of SAEs as an unsupervised tool for enhancing both interpretability and control of VLMs. Code and benchmark data are available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/sae-for-vlm.

papers.title: Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages
papers.research_question: What are the abilities and inabilities of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in interpreting language models, and how can we make them learn causally relevant features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes SAEs on formal languages, showing that while they can find interpretable features, these features often lack causal impact, and proposes a causal regularization method to incentivize learning of causally relevant features.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality should be a central target in SAE training, and the proposed method is a proof-of-concept step towards learning causally relevant features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can identify interpretable latents corresponding to grammar features like depth and parts-of-speech.
SAE performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like regularization and normalization.
Interpretable features from standard SAEs do not necessarily have causal effects on model outputs.
The proposed causal regularization method can lead to SAE features with predictable causal impacts.
Top-k regularization outperforms L1 regularization in finding interpretable features.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method is a proof-of-concept and only tested on synthetic formal languages.
The method relies on the availability of correlated tokens for weak supervision, which may not always be present in real-world settings.
future_direction: Overcoming the limitation of relying on correlated tokens
Extending the method to real-world settings
papers.abstract: Autoencoders have been used for finding interpretable and disentangled features underlying neural network representations in both image and text domains. While the efficacy and pitfalls of such methods are well-studied in vision, there is a lack of corresponding results, both qualitative and quantitative, for the text domain. We aim to address this gap by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on a synthetic testbed of formal languages. Specifically, we train SAEs on the hidden representations of models trained on formal languages (Dyck-2, Expr, and English PCFG) under a wide variety of hyperparameter settings, finding interpretable latents often emerge in the features learned by our SAEs. However, similar to vision, we find performance turns out to be highly sensitive to inductive biases of the training pipeline. Moreover, we show latents correlating to certain features of the input do not always induce a causal impact on model's computation. We thus argue that causality has to become a central target in SAE training: learning of causal features should be incentivized from the ground-up. Motivated by this, we propose and perform preliminary investigations for an approach that promotes learning of causally relevant features in our formal language setting.

papers.title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstractions are learned by neurons in deep models? Do compositional explanations give insight into model performance? Can they be used to predictably manipulate model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a procedure for generating compositional logical explanations of individual neurons, which provides more precise and expressive characterizations of neuron behavior than atomic labels, and applies it to analyze vision and NLP models.
papers.conclusion: Compositional explanations offer a more precise and expressive way to characterize neuron behavior, providing insights into model performance and enabling targeted adversarial manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons learn compositional concepts: in image classification, some learn meaningful perceptual abstractions while others are polysemantic; in NLI, shallow heuristics (e.g., based on gender, lexical overlap) are reified in individual neurons.
The interpretability of neurons correlates differently with performance: in image classification, human-interpretable abstractions are positively correlated with accuracy, while in NLI, neurons explained by shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with accuracy.
Compositional explanations enable the creation of simple 'copy-paste' adversarial examples that predictably change model behavior by targeting specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
The method requires technical expertise to implement, limiting usability by non-experts.
It relies on annotated datasets which may be expensive to collect and may be biased in the features they contain or omit.
Neuron-level explanations cannot identify concepts distributed across multiple neurons or establish definitive causal chains between inputs and decisions.
future_direction: Building easier user interfaces for explainability.
Reducing data annotation requirements.
Extending composition operators (e.g., to relations like ABOVE and BELOW) and applying the method to other tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.

papers.title: Replicating Circuit Tracing for a Simple Known Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) recover known computational mechanisms in GPT-2 Small for the greater-than task, and what interpretable features do they discover?
papers.core_contribution: CLTs can identify interpretable computational components in well-understood tasks, replicating prior findings while revealing novel features like abstract parity detectors, though with differences in representation compared to non-sparse methods.
papers.conclusion: CLTs demonstrate the ability to semi-autonomously discover interesting structure in language models, validating their use for circuit analysis while highlighting differences in sparse versus non-sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
CLTs successfully identify relevant and interpretable features for the greater-than task, including greater-than features similar to prior work.
Discovered features include abstract parity features that promote even-numbered predictions and suppress odd-numbered ones, indicating richer representational structures.
Some CLT features show less input dependence or more specialized behavior compared to features found by Hanna et al.
Discrepancies exist between logit attribution heatmaps and max-activating examples for some features, possibly due to feature interaction effects.
CLTs can uncover relevant structure without labor-intensive experimental interventions used in prior work.
papers.limitation:
discrepancies between logit attribution heatmaps and max-activating examples for some features
feature selection based on a single prompt may not isolate the cleanest circuit
future_direction: Studying interactions between token positions using CLTs' ability to trace cross-position interactions.
Understanding how CLT number representations relate to non-sparse model representations like helical representations.
papers.abstract: Can Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) recover known computational mechanisms in GPT-2 Small for the greater-than task, and what interpretable features do they discover? CLTs can identify interpretable computational components in well-understood tasks, replicating prior findings while revealing novel features like abstract parity detectors, though with differences in representation compared to non-sparse methods. CLTs demonstrate the ability to semi-autonomously discover interesting structure in language models, validating their use for circuit analysis while highlighting differences in sparse versus non-sparse representations.

papers.title: Local vs distributed representations: What is the right basis for interpretability?
papers.research_question: Are dictionary-based representations more interpretable than neuron-based representations for understanding convolutional neural networks, and how does the choice of representational basis affect model comparisons?
papers.core_contribution: Dictionary-based representations are consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations in CNNs, and model comparisons based solely on neuron-level analyses can be misleading due to differences in superposition.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary-based representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, and comparing models using only neuron-based representations can lead to misleading conclusions about their relative interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations across three psychophysics experiments, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.
ResNet50 exhibits greater superposition (lower axis-alignment) than VGG16, which masks its higher interpretability in neuron-based comparisons.
ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 when evaluated using dictionary-based representations, but this difference disappears when using neuron-based representations.
Dictionary elements are at least as decision-relevant as individual neurons, as measured by Gradient×Input importance.
papers.limitation:
The experimental protocol may be confounded by semantics, as participants could solve trials by simple semantic grouping rather than identifying visual patterns.
The study is limited to two CNN architectures (ResNet50 and VGG16).
future_direction: Further refinement of the experimental protocol to better mitigate semantic confounds.
Examination of the interpretability of dictionary elements recovered by applying dictionary learning to full layer activations.
Expanding the range of architectures to understand why certain models are inherently more interpretable than others.
papers.abstract: Much of the research on the interpretability of deep neural networks has focused on studying the visual features that maximally activate individual neurons. However, recent work has cast doubts on the usefulness of such local representations for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks because individual neurons tend to respond to multiple unrelated visual patterns, a phenomenon referred to as "superposition". A promising alternative to disentangle these complex patterns is learning sparsely distributed vector representations from entire network layers, as the resulting basis vectors seemingly encode single identifiable visual patterns consistently. Thus, one would expect the resulting code to align better with human perceivable visual patterns, but supporting evidence remains, at best, anecdotal. To fill this gap, we conducted three large-scale psychophysics experiments collected from a pool of 560 participants. Our findings provide (i) strong evidence that features obtained from sparse distributed representations are easier to interpret by human observers and (ii) that this effect is more pronounced in the deepest layers of a neural network. Complementary analyses also reveal that (iii) features derived from sparse distributed representations contribute more to the model's decision. Overall, our results highlight that distributed representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, underscoring a need for the field to move beyond the interpretation of local neural codes in favor of sparsely distributed ones.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: No One-Size-Fits-All Neurons: Task-based Neurons for Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Since the human brain is a task-based neuron user, can artificial network design go from task-based architecture design to task-based neuron design? Can we design different neurons for different tasks (task-based neurons)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a two-step framework using vectorized symbolic regression to design task-based neurons, which enhances feature representation for specific tasks and outperforms networks with universal neurons.
papers.conclusion: Task-based neuron design is a feasible and promising new dimension in deep learning, offering competitive performance by incorporating task-specific inductive biases into the neuronal aggregation function.
papers.key_findings:
Task-based neurons designed via vectorized symbolic regression capture underlying data patterns and, when formed into networks, outperform linear and preset quadratic neurons on tabular data.
The proposed vectorized symbolic regression is computationally efficient, supports parallel computation, and avoids overfitting compared to traditional symbolic regression.
Task-based networks achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art models like XGBoost, LightGBM, and specialized tabular deep learning models on real-world tasks such as particle collision prediction.
The framework is flexible and can be extended beyond polynomial base functions to include trigonometric and exponential functions, allowing adaptation to diverse data characteristics.
Experiments on synthetic and public datasets confirm the feasibility, necessity, and superiority of task-based neuron design.
future_direction: Extend the search space of vectorized symbolic regression to include trigonometric and exponential functions to better capture data with specific physical significance.
Include more base functions and let the symbolic regression automatically select the optimal expression, given sufficient computational resources.
Explore the application of task-based neurons beyond tabular data to other data modalities and network architectures.
papers.abstract: Biologically, the brain does not rely on a single type of neuron that universally functions in all aspects. Instead, it acts as a sophisticated designer of task-based neurons. In this study, we address the following question: since the human brain is a task-based neuron user, can the artificial network design go from the task-based architecture design to the task-based neuron design? Since methodologically there are no one-size-fits-all neurons, given the same structure, task-based neurons can enhance the feature representation ability relative to the existing universal neurons due to the intrinsic inductive bias for the task. Specifically, we propose a two-step framework for prototyping task-based neurons. First, symbolic regression is used to identify optimal formulas that fit input data by utilizing base functions such as logarithmic, trigonometric, and exponential functions. We introduce vectorized symbolic regression that stacks all variables in a vector and regularizes each input variable to perform the same computation, which can expedite the regression speed, facilitate parallel computation, and avoid overfitting. Second, we parameterize the acquired elementary formula to make parameters learnable, which serves as the aggregation function of the neuron. The activation functions such as ReLU and the sigmoidal functions remain the same because they have proven to be good. Empirically, experimental results on synthetic data, classic benchmarks, and real-world applications show that the proposed task-based neuron design is not only feasible but also delivers competitive performance over other state-of-the-art models.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Towards Universality: Studying Mechanistic Similarity Across Language Model Architectures
papers.research_question: Does mechanistic understanding transfer across different model architectures? Specifically, how similar are the features and circuits in Transformer and Mamba models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer and Mamba models learn similar interpretable features as extracted by Sparse Autoencoders, and their induction circuits are structurally analogous, with a nuanced Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that SAE feature similarity is a useful measure for cross-architectural universality, revealing significant similarity between Transformer and Mamba features and circuits, with an Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE features in Pythia and Mamba are similar, with high Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (MPPC).
Feature similarity is affected by semantic complexity; simpler features have higher correlation.
Induction circuits in Mamba are analogous to those in Transformers, but with an Off-by-One motif where information is written into the SSM state at the next token.
SAE features show depth specialization across architectures, with matched features appearing at proportionally similar layers.
The neuron baseline shows almost zero similarity, indicating SAEs are better for cross-architecture comparison than neuron-based methods.
papers.limitation:
SAEs may not capture all true features and might capture combinations of features rather than the features themselves.
Circuit universality analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative automated comparison tools.
future_direction: Automating circuit discovery and comparison for quantitative measurement of circuit universality.
Further study on the Off-by-One motif in Mamba circuits to understand its purpose and formation.
papers.abstract: The hypothesis of Universality in interpretability suggests that different neural networks may converge to implement similar algorithms on similar tasks. In this work, we investigate two mainstream architectures for language modeling, namely Transformers and Mambas, to explore the extent of their mechanistic similarity. We propose to use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to isolate interpretable features from these models and show that most features are similar in these two models. We also validate the correlation between feature similarity and Universality. We then delve into the circuit-level analysis of Mamba models and find that the induction circuits in Mamba are structurally analogous to those in Transformers. We also identify a nuanced difference we call \emph{Off-by-One motif}: The information of one token is written into the SSM state in its next position. Whilst interaction between tokens in Transformers does not exhibit such trend.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: From deep learning to mechanistic understanding in neuroscience: the structure of retinal prediction
papers.research_question: How can we systematically extract computational mechanisms from deep neural network models of biological sensory processing, and do these mechanisms match those in the brain?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic model reduction approach combining dimensionality reduction and attribution methods to extract computational mechanisms from deep CNN models of the retina, revealing how the retina acts as a predictive feature extractor.
papers.conclusion: Deep CNN models combined with model reduction can yield conceptual insights into computational mechanisms in the brain, and in the retina, a single model with multiple nonlinear pathways can explain diverse retinal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
For omitted stimulus response, a reduced model with three pathways (1 OFF, 2 ON) explains the shift in burst peak with flash frequency.
For latency coding, a dual pathway mechanism of slow ON and fast OFF bipolar cells explains the latency shift.
For motion reversal, two channels with nonlinear interactions explain the burst and fixed latency.
For motion anticipation, direction-sensitive inhibition truncates the lagging edge, shifting the peak forward.
The approach validates deep CNNs as a method for generating veridical scientific hypotheses about neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Systematic exploration of universality and individuality across different model initializations, architectures, and recordings.
Extending the model reduction procedure to obtain multilayer reduced models for deeper CNNs of higher cortical regions.
Using complex models to design new stimuli that elucidate functional reasons for model complexity.
papers.abstract: Recently, deep feedforward neural networks have achieved considerable success in modeling biological sensory processing, in terms of reproducing the input-output map of sensory neurons. However, such models raise profound questions about the very nature of explanation in neuroscience. Are we simply replacing one complex system (a biological circuit) with another (a deep network), without understanding either? Moreover, beyond neural representations, are the deep network's computational mechanisms for generating neural responses the same as those in the brain? Without a systematic approach to extracting and understanding computational mechanisms from deep neural network models, it can be difficult both to assess the degree of utility of deep learning approaches in neuroscience, and to extract experimentally testable hypotheses from deep networks. We develop such a systematic approach by combining dimensionality reduction and modern attribution methods for determining the relative importance of interneurons for specific visual computations. We apply this approach to deep network models of the retina, revealing a conceptual understanding of how the retina acts as a predictive feature extractor that signals deviations from expectations for diverse spatiotemporal stimuli. For each stimulus, our extracted computational mechanisms are consistent with prior scientific literature, and in one case yields a new mechanistic hypothesis. Thus overall, this work not only yields insights into the computational mechanisms underlying the striking predictive capabilities of the retina, but also places the framework of deep networks as neuroscientific models on firmer theoretical foundations, by providing a new roadmap to go beyond comparing neural representations to extracting and understand computational mechanisms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Circuits: Grokking as Competition of Sparse and Dense Subnetworks
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism behind the grokking phase transition in neural networks, specifically how does competition between subnetworks lead to generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The grokking phase transition arises from competition between a sparse subnetwork and a dense subnetwork, driven by selective norm growth of neurons in the sparse subnetwork.
papers.conclusion: Grokking in neural networks is driven by competition between sparse and dense subnetworks, with selective norm growth leading to the emergence of a generalizing sparse subnetwork.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking corresponds to network sparsification, with a sparse subnetwork emerging to dominate predictions.
Selective norm growth of specific neurons induces sparsity during the grokking transition.
The sparse subnetwork competes with and eventually surpasses the dense subnetwork in controlling model output.
The size of the sparse subnetwork matches disjunctive normal form circuit sizes for computing parity.
Before grokking, the network may generalize based on task properties like commutativity, not just memorization.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to the specific setting of the sparse parity task.
future_direction: Extend analysis of grokking to large language models.
papers.abstract: Grokking is a phenomenon where a model trained on an algorithmic task first overfits but, then, after a large amount of additional training, undergoes a phase transition to generalize perfectly. We empirically study the internal structure of networks undergoing grokking on the sparse parity task, and find that the grokking phase transition corresponds to the emergence of a sparse subnetwork that dominates model predictions. On an optimization level, we find that this subnetwork arises when a small subset of neurons undergoes rapid norm growth, whereas the other neurons in the network decay slowly in norm. Thus, we suggest that the grokking phase transition can be understood to emerge from competition of two largely distinct subnetworks: a dense one that dominates before the transition and generalizes poorly, and a sparse one that dominates afterwards.

papers.title: Circuit-Tracer: A New Library for Finding Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we facilitate feature-circuit finding in LLMs? The paper introduces a library to make circuit analysis more accessible.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tracer, an open-source library for efficient identification, visualization, and intervention on feature circuits in LLMs, making circuit analysis more accessible.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents circuit-tracer, a library that enables efficient feature circuit tracing, and demonstrates its utility through case studies, aiming to facilitate future research in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Transcoder circuits often fail to capture features relevant to attention, as edge weights are conditioned on the attention pattern.
Transcoder errors can hinder interpretation when a large proportion of the flow through the graph originates from uninterpretable error nodes.
future_direction: Systematic study of safety-relevant phenomena such as chain of thought unfaithfulness, refusal, and jailbreaks using circuits.
Synthesizing multiple circuits into a coherent task mechanism.
Scaling feature annotation and supernode creation.
papers.abstract: Feature circuits aim to shed light on LLM behavior by identifying the features that are causally responsible for a given LLM output, and connecting them into a directed graph, or *circuit*, that explains how both each feature and each output arose. However, performing circuit analysis is challenging: the tools for finding, visualizing, and verifying feature circuits are complex and spread across multiple libraries.To facilitate feature-circuit finding, we introduce `circuit-tracer`, an open-source library for efficient identification of feature circuits. `circuit-tracer` provides an integrated pipeline for finding, visualizing, annotating, and performing interventions on such feature circuits, tested with various model sizes, up to 14B parameters. We make `circuit-tracer` available to both developers and end users, via integration with tools such as Neuronpedia, which provides a user-friendly interface.

papers.title: Encoding and Understanding Astrophysical Information in Large Language Model-Generated Summaries
papers.research_question: To what extent does prompt engineering affect the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities, and how is physics information encoded in text summaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can encode physical information from astrophysical text, with structured prompting improving alignment between embeddings and physical quantities, and sparse autoencoders reveal the semantic concepts driving this encoding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can capture, learn, and represent physics concepts in textual data, and prompt engineering enhances the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities. Sparse autoencoders provide insight into the semantic concepts underlying this encoding.
papers.key_findings:
Structured prompts significantly improve the clustering purity of LLM embeddings with respect to physical quantities, with improvements up to 57.5% for variability index.
Sparse autoencoders extract interpretable features from text embeddings that correlate with specific astrophysical properties, such as non-thermal characteristics linked to power-law gamma values.
LLMs infer physical parameters from text descriptions even when numerical values are not explicitly stated, demonstrating an understanding of astrophysical concepts.
Concepts like 'eclipsing binaries' and 'galaxy cluster thermal dynamics' are encoded in the embeddings and associated with physical measurements.
The method allows for visual and quantitative analysis of how physics is encoded in language through t-SNE clustering and SAE feature activation.
future_direction: Expanding the dataset to include more sources
Optimizing prompting with different models
Creating an interface for astronomer validation of possibly anomalous objects
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated the ability to generalize well at many levels across domains, modalities, and even shown in-context learning capabilities. This enables research questions regarding how they can be used to encode physical information that is usually only available from scientific measurements, and loosely encoded in textual descriptions. Using astrophysics as a test bed, we investigate if LLM embeddings can codify physical summary statistics that are obtained from scientific measurements through two main questions: 1) Does prompting play a role on how those quantities are codified by the LLM? and 2) What aspects of language are most important in encoding the physics represented by the measurement? We investigate this using sparse autoencoders that extract interpretable features from the text.

papers.title: Preserving Bilinear Weight Spectra with a Signed and Shrunk Quadratic Activation Function
papers.research_question: Can we design an activation function for Gated Linear Units (GLUs) that enables weight-based interpretability (via eigen-features) without sacrificing performance and data efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function for GLUs that preserves the weight structure properties of bilinear MLPs (enabling interpretability via eigen-decomposition) while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions.
papers.conclusion: Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS) is an activation function that enables the development of interpretable features via weight spectra while providing performance on par with, and in some scenarios better than, standard activation functions.
papers.key_findings:
SQS-GLU learns interpretable features, as shown by eigenvector decomposition of its weight matrices, similar to bilinear MLPs.
SQS achieves performance (loss, accuracy, perplexity) competitive with or better than ReLU, GELU, and SwiGLU on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Tiny Stories.
SQS converges faster and achieves lower loss than ReLU-GLUs and Bilinear MLPs on the image classification tasks.
The eigenvectors from SQS-GLU show high cosine similarity with those from Bilinear MLPs, indicating preserved interpretability.
SQS maintains computational efficiency comparable to other activation functions when implemented with specific hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of machine learning models is critical for ensuring their reliability and robustness. Whilst many techniques in mechanistic interpretability focus on activation driven analyses, being able to derive meaningful features directly from the weights of a neural network would provide greater guarantees and more computational efficiency. Existing techniques for analyzing model features through weights suffer from drawbacks such as reduced performance and data inefficiency. In this paper, we introduce Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function designed to allow Gated Linear Units (GLUs) to learn interpretable features without these drawbacks. Our experimental results show that SQS achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions whilst enabling weight-based interpretability

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Stable and Interpretable Unrolled Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can unrolled sparse coding networks be used for provable dictionary learning, addressing biased code estimates and gradient instability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PUDLE, a provable unrolled dictionary learning method with theoretical guarantees on code support recovery and gradient stability, and demonstrates interpretability.
papers.conclusion: PUDLE enables stable and interpretable dictionary learning with theoretical convergence guarantees, and outperforms existing methods in dictionary recovery and image denoising.
papers.key_findings:
Unrolled sparse coding can recover and preserve the correct code support under proper initialization and regularization.
Using reconstruction loss in backpropagation (gae-ls_t) mitigates bias propagation and leads to better dictionary recovery compared to other gradient estimates.
Proper dictionary initialization and loss choice resolve gradient instability in unrolled networks.
The unrolled network is interpretable, with mathematical relations between learned dictionary, sparse codes, and training data.
PUDLE outperforms NOODL and SPORCO in dictionary learning and image denoising tasks.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions like finite-iteration support selection and strong convexity, which may be stringent for generalization beyond dictionary learning.
The analysis is conducted in the noiseless setting; extension to noisy measurements is left for future work.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis to other min-min optimization problems like ridge regression and logistic regression.
Extend the analysis to noisy settings.
Derive finite-sample bounds for dictionary learning with unrolled networks.
papers.abstract: The dictionary learning problem, representing data as a combination of a few atoms, has long stood as a popular method for learning representations in statistics and signal processing. The most popular dictionary learning algorithm alternates between sparse coding and dictionary update steps, and a rich literature has studied its theoretical convergence. The success of dictionary learning relies on access to a "good" initial estimate of the dictionary and the ability of the sparse coding step to provide an unbiased estimate of the code. The growing popularity of unrolled sparse coding networks has led to the empirical finding that backpropagation through such networks performs dictionary learning. We offer the theoretical analysis of these empirical results through PUDLE, a Provable Unrolled Dictionary LEarning method. We provide conditions on the network initialization and data distribution sufficient to recover and preserve the support of the latent code. Additionally, we address two challenges; first, the vanilla unrolled sparse coding computes a biased code estimate, and second, gradients during backpropagated learning can become unstable. We show approaches to reduce the bias of the code estimate in the forward pass, and that of the dictionary estimate in the backward pass. We propose strategies to resolve the learning instability by tuning network parameters and modifying the loss function. Overall, we highlight the impact of loss, unrolling, and backpropagation on convergence. We complement our findings through synthetic and image denoising experiments. Finally, we demonstrate PUDLE's interpretability, a driving factor in designing deep networks based on iterative optimizations, by building a mathematical relation between network weights, its output, and the training set.

papers.title: Task-Specific Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Monosemantic Neuronal Activations
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently select data subsets from general instruction datasets to maximize LLM performance on targeted tasks, given only a handful of target examples?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MONA, a model-centric data selection method for instruction tuning that uses sparse autoencoders to derive monosemantic neuronal activation embeddings, enabling more semantically aligned and interpretable selection of task-relevant data.
papers.conclusion: MONA provides a model-centric approach for task-specific data selection in instruction tuning, using monosemantic neuronal activations to capture internal model computation, leading to more semantically aligned and interpretable data selection and consistent performance gains.
papers.key_findings:
MONA consistently outperforms existing data selection baselines (influence-based and distribution alignment) across multiple instruction datasets, evaluation tasks, models, and data selection ratios.
Disentangling polysemantic neuron activations into monosemantic representations via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) yields clearer task-specific activation patterns and improves data selection quality.
The proposed generalized Jaccard similarity metric is more effective than Euclidean or Cosine similarity in the sparse monosemantic activation space.
Using mean aggregation (length normalization) for token-level activations is crucial to mitigate length bias in sample embedding.
An LLM-based data analyst evaluation confirms that MONA selects data with higher semantic relevance and format alignment to target tasks.
papers.abstract: Instruction tuning improves the ability of large language models (LLMs) to follow diverse human instructions, but achieving strong performance on specific target tasks remains challenging. A critical bottleneck is selecting the most relevant data to maximize task-specific performance. Existing data selection approaches include unstable influence-based methods and more stable distribution alignment methods, the latter of which critically rely on the underlying sample representation. In practice, most distribution alignment methods, from shallow features (e.g., BM25) to neural embeddings (e.g., BGE, LLM2Vec), may fail to capture how the model internally processes samples. To bridge this gap, we adopt a model-centric strategy in which each sample is represented by its neuronal activation pattern in the model, directly reflecting internal computation. However, directly using raw neuron activations leads to spurious similarity between unrelated samples due to neuron polysemanticity, where a single neuron may respond to multiple, unrelated concepts. To address this, we employ sparse autoencoders to disentangle polysemantic activations into sparse, monosemantic representations, and introduce a dedicated similarity metric for this space to better identify task-relevant data. Comprehensive experiments across multiple instruction datasets, models, tasks, and selection ratios show that our approach consistently outperforms existing data selection baselines in both stability and task-specific performance.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand and steer the internal mechanisms of CLIP's vision transformer, and what differences exist between vision and language processing in these models?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on CLIP's vision transformer to interpret and steer its features, revealing differences between vision and language processing, and demonstrating improved performance on vision disentanglement tasks and typographic attack defense.
papers.conclusion: SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer reveal sparsity differences and provide steerable features that enable improved disentanglement and state-of-the-art defense against typographic attacks.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs on CLIP show distinct sparsity patterns for spatial vs CLS tokens and compared to language models.
10-15% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model.
Targeted suppression of SAE features improves performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, typographic attacks).
Optimal disentanglement occurs in middle layers.
State-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.
papers.limitation:
The steerability metric does not capture semantic relationships between promoted concepts.
Some features may not be accurately captured due to limited vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Improving the steerability metric to capture semantic relationships between concepts.
Exploring larger vocabularies to better capture feature semantics.
papers.abstract: While vision models are highly capable, their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood -- a challenge which sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have helped address in language, but which remains underexplored in vision. We address this gap by training SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer and uncover key differences between vision and language processing, including distinct sparsity patterns for SAEs trained across layers and token types. We then provide the first systematic analysis on the steerability of CLIP's vision transformer by introducing metrics to quantify how precisely SAE features can be steered to affect the model's output. We find that 10-15\% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model. Through targeted suppression of SAE features, we then demonstrate improved performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, and typographic attacks), finding optimal disentanglement in middle model layers, and achieving state-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.

papers.title: CXR-LanIC: Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
papers.research_question: How to make chest X-ray diagnosis models interpretable for clinical adoption by providing transparent, verifiable explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CXR-LanIC, a framework for interpretable chest X-ray diagnosis through task-aligned pattern discovery using transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP classifier.
papers.conclusion: CXR-LanIC addresses the black-box problem in medical AI by providing interpretable patterns, achieving competitive accuracy, and supporting safer clinical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Discovers approximately 5,000 monosemantic visual patterns spanning clinical categories through transcoder ensembles.
Achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing interpretable explanations.
Demonstrates that task-aligned pattern discovery from classifier embeddings yields clinically relevant features.
papers.limitation: Patterns currently lack natural language descriptions, requiring future LMM-based annotation.
future_direction: Complete LMM-based annotation of patterns to generate natural language explanations.
Validate explanation quality through LMM verification and radiologist evaluation.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable accuracy in chest X-ray diagnosis, yet their widespread clinical adoption remains limited by the black-box nature of their predictions. Clinicians require transparent, verifiable explanations to trust automated diagnoses and identify potential failure modes. We introduce CXR-LanIC (Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-rays), a novel framework that addresses this interpretability challenge through task-aligned pattern discovery. Our approach trains transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP diagnostic classifier to decompose medical image representations into interpretable visual patterns. By training an ensemble of 100 transcoders on multimodal embeddings from the MIMIC-CXR dataset, we discover approximately 5,000 monosemantic patterns spanning cardiac, pulmonary, pleural, structural, device, and artifact categories. Each pattern exhibits consistent activation behavior across images sharing specific radiological features, enabling transparent attribution where predictions decompose into 20-50 interpretable patterns with verifiable activation galleries. CXR-LanIC achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing the foundation for natural language explanations through planned large multimodal model annotation. Our key innovation lies in extracting interpretable features from a classifier trained on specific diagnostic objectives rather than general-purpose embeddings, ensuring discovered patterns are directly relevant to clinical decision-making, demonstrating that medical AI systems can be both accurate and interpretable, supporting safer clinical deployment through transparent, clinically grounded explanations.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
