papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Closed-Form Interpretation of Neural Network Classifiers with Symbolic Gradients
papers.research_question: Is it possible to extract a human-readable concept that is learned by a neural network by getting rid of the elusive transformation that conceals it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for interpreting neural network classifiers by embedding them into an equivalence class of functions that encode the same concept and finding an intersection with human-readable equations via symbolic search on gradients.
papers.conclusion: The introduced framework effectively interprets neural network classifiers by extracting closed-form expressions of the concepts they learn, moving beyond mere output replication.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully recovers the exact closed-form decision boundary function in several synthetic binary classification experiments.
The method reveals that a neural network can learn a combination of high-level features, whereas direct symbolic classification may only capture one feature.
The interpretation is based on matching normalized gradients, which avoids the need to replicate the neural network's output directly.
papers.limitation:
The method cannot learn functions of a single variable because it reduces the concept to a one-dimensional function.
The method loses the numerical value of the threshold/bias of the output neuron.
The framework is more useful in bottleneck layers and when neurons are disentangled, as it cannot capture information distributed among multiple neurons.
papers.abstract: I introduce a unified framework for finding a closed-form interpretation of any single neuron in an artificial neural network. Using this framework I demonstrate how to interpret neural network classifiers to reveal closed-form expressions of the concepts encoded in their decision boundaries. In contrast to neural network-based regression, for classification, it is in general impossible to express the neural network in the form of a symbolic equation even if the neural network itself bases its classification on a quantity that can be written as a closed-form equation. The interpretation framework is based on embedding trained neural networks into an equivalence class of functions that encode the same concept. I interpret these neural networks by finding an intersection between the equivalence class and human-readable equations defined by a symbolic search space. The approach is not limited to classifiers or full neural networks and can be applied to arbitrary neurons in hidden layers or latent spaces.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the extent and causes of parameter update sparsity induced by reinforcement learning fine-tuning in large language models, comparing it to supervised fine-tuning.
papers.core_contribution: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning in large language models updates only a small, sparse subnetwork of parameters (5%-30%) without explicit sparsity constraints, and fine-tuning this subnetwork alone can recover the performance and nearly identical parameters of the fully fine-tuned model.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning in LLMs naturally updates only a sparse subnetwork, driven by in-distribution training, enabling efficient recovery of full model performance via subnetwork-only fine-tuning and suggesting more efficient training strategies.
papers.key_findings:
RL induces sparse parameter updates (68.5% to 96% sparsity) across diverse algorithms and models without explicit regularization, while SFT induces dense updates.
Updates are distributed across all transformer layers and parameter matrices (Q, K, V, FFN) except layer normalization, which is rarely updated, and are sparse but full-rank.
Fine-tuning only the identified sparse subnetwork recovers the test accuracy and converges to nearly identical parameter values as the fully fine-tuned model.
Subnetworks show substantially higher overlap than random chance across different random seeds, training data, and RL algorithms, indicating a partially transferable structure.
The primary driver of update sparsity is training on in-distribution data (close to the policy distribution), while KL regularization and gradient clipping have limited impact.
papers.limitation:
The study varies one factor at a time, but the observed sparsity may result from complex interactions among many factors.
Fully controlled experiments are computationally prohibitive, leading to reliance on public checkpoints in some cases.
Experiments focus on language models; extending the analysis to multimodal and diffusion models is left for future work.
The empirical findings invite deeper theoretical analysis to explain the update sparsity phenomenon.
There are confounders (e.g., Liu et al. 2025a) that are not trivial and worth exploring in future work.
future_direction: Examine complex interactions among multiple factors contributing to update sparsity.
Explore the same sparsity phenomena in multimodal and diffusion models.
Investigate methods for early identification of the sparse subnetwork and leverage its structure for more efficient learning.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) yields substantial improvements in large language models (LLMs) downstream task performance and alignment with human values. Surprisingly, such large gains result from updating only a small subnetwork comprising just 5 percent to 30 percent of the parameters, with the rest effectively unchanged. We refer to this phenomenon as parameter update sparsity induced by RL. It is observed across all 7 widely used RL algorithms (e.g., PPO, GRPO, DPO) and all 10 LLMs from different families in our experiments. This sparsity is intrinsic and occurs without any explicit sparsity promoting regularizations or architectural constraints. Finetuning the subnetwork alone recovers the test accuracy, and, remarkably, produces a model nearly identical to the one obtained via full finetuning. The subnetworks from different random seeds, training data, and even RL algorithms show substantially greater overlap than expected by chance. Our analysis suggests that this sparsity is not due to updating only a subset of layers, instead, nearly all parameter matrices receive similarly sparse updates. Moreover, the updates to almost all parameter matrices are nearly full-rank, suggesting RL updates a small subset of parameters that nevertheless span almost the full subspaces that the parameter matrices can represent. We conjecture that the this update sparsity can be primarily attributed to training on data that is near the policy distribution, techniques that encourage the policy to remain close to the pretrained model, such as the KL regularization and gradient clipping, have limited impact.

papers.title: Line of Sight: On Linear Representations in VLLMs
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models represent images in their hidden activations? Are VLLM representations of visual concepts novel and distinct from existing LLM representations, or are they simply superficial extensions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that image concepts are linearly represented in the residual stream of a VLLM, demonstrates the causality of these representations via steering interventions, and introduces multimodal SAEs to discover interpretable features, showing that representations become increasingly shared across modalities in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that image concepts are linearly represented in VLLMs, enabling fine-grained control, and that representations become increasingly multimodal in deeper layers, with neurons forming an interpretable basis for image information.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can accurately classify ImageNet classes from mean residual stream embeddings, achieving performance competitive with self-supervised image classifiers.
Steering vectors derived from image classes can causally edit model outputs, with interventions in early to middle layers being most effective.
Image information is transferred to text tokens in early-mid layers; ablating image tokens after layer 12 has negligible effect on model coherence.
Text-derived features (Logit Lens and Text Embeddings) are ineffective for steering image representations, indicating disjoint representations early on.
Multimodal SAEs yield interpretable, monosemantic features for both text and images, with features becoming more multimodal in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Linear representations provide an unnatural basis for image-space adversarial attacks, as adversarial perturbations are dense and not well-explained by SAE features.
SAEs suffer from distributional shift when applied to all tokens, causing accuracy to drop to near chance on complex VQA tasks.
Adversarial attacks are brittle and do not generalize well across different prompts.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms underlying image-to-multimodal representation conversion.
Evaluate these findings across diverse VLLM architectures, particularly cross-attention-based models.
papers.abstract: Language models can be equipped with multimodal capabilities by fine-tuning on embeddings of visual inputs. But how do such multimodal models represent images in their hidden activations? We explore representations of image concepts within LlaVA-Next, a popular open-source VLLM. We find a diverse set of ImageNet classes represented via linearly decodable features in the residual stream. We show that the features are causal by performing targeted edits on the model output. In order to increase the diversity of the studied linear features, we train multimodal Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), creating a highly interpretable dictionary of text and image features. We find that although model representations across modalities are quite disjoint, they become increasingly shared in deeper layers.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: LUCID-SAE: Learning Unified Vision-Language Sparse Codes for Interpretable Concept Discovery
papers.research_question: Can we learn a single set of sparse codes whose units are directly comparable across vision and language spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LUCID, a unified vision-language sparse autoencoder that learns a shared latent dictionary for image patch and text token representations, enabling cross-modal feature alignment and automatic concept interpretation.
papers.conclusion: LUCID establishes aligned sparse dictionaries as a foundation for automatic interpretability at scale, providing a principled approach toward interpretable multimodal representations that support systematic cross-modal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Shared-private decomposition improves both reconstruction fidelity and cross-modal predictability by shielding the shared space from modality-specific noise.
Optimal transport-based alignment enables precise patch-level grounding as measured by local spatial metrics.
Structured shared-code objectives mitigate clustering degeneracy while sharpening object-level grounding.
LUCID captures diverse concept categories spanning objects, scenes, actions, attributes, and spatial relationships, with learned representations generalizing to out-of-distribution data.
An automated neuron interpretation pipeline discovers coherent semantic clusters without manual annotation.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a natural path toward comparable explanations across different representation spaces. However, current SAEs are trained per modality, producing dictionaries whose features are not directly understandable and whose explanations do not transfer across domains. In this study, we introduce LUCID (Learning Unified vision-language sparse Codes for Interpretable concept Discovery), a unified vision-language sparse autoencoder that learns a shared latent dictionary for image patch and text token representations, while reserving private capacity for modality-specific details. We achieve feature alignment by coupling the shared codes with a learned optimal transport matching objective without the need of labeling. LUCID yields interpretable shared features that support patch-level grounding, establish cross-modal neuron correspondence, and enhance robustness against the concept clustering problem in similarity-based evaluation. Leveraging the alignment properties, we develop an automated dictionary interpretation pipeline based on term clustering without manual observations. Our analysis reveals that LUCID's shared features capture diverse semantic categories beyond objects, including actions, attributes, and abstract concepts, demonstrating a comprehensive approach to interpretable multimodal representations.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Toward Knowledge Extraction in Classification of Volcano-Seismic Events: Visualizing Hidden States in Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we understand what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model in the context of volcano-seismic event classification, and how can this knowledge be used to improve data interpretation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces visualization approaches to understand the hidden state dynamics of RNNs in volcano-seismic event classification, showing how neuron specialization varies with architecture and event type, and how this can be used for network pruning and active learning.
papers.conclusion: The visualization approaches help understand RNN internal mechanisms, and neuron specialization can be used for network pruning and active learning in volcano-seismic event classification.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM architectures exhibit lower neuronal activity and better specialization compared to Vanilla RNN.
Neurons specialize for specific events and frequency bands, which can be visualized through activation maps.
The degree of specialization allows for network pruning (removing less specialized neurons) without significant performance loss.
LSTM architectures are more stable and have higher susceptibility to changes in input compared to Vanilla RNN.
future_direction: Exploring the correlation between dropout and specialization of neurons.
Using neuron specialization for active learning and network sparsity.
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep hierarchical models build their knowledge is a key issue in the usage of artificial intelligence to interpret the reality behind data. Depending on the discipline and models used, such knowledge may be represented in ways that are more or less intelligible for humans, limiting further improvements on the performance of the existing models. In order to delve into the characterization and modeling of volcano-seismic signals, this article emphasizes the idea of deciphering what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model, and how this knowledge can be used to improve data interpretation. The key to accomplishing these objectives is both analyzing the hidden state dynamics associated with their hidden units as well as pruning/trimming based on the specialization of neurons. In this article, we process, analyze, and visualize the hidden states activation maps of two RNN architectures when managing different types of volcano-seismic events. As a result, the class-dependent discriminative behavior of most active neurons is analyzed, thereby increasing the comprehension of the detection and classification tasks. A representative dataset from the deception island volcano (Antarctica), containing volcano-tectonic earthquakes, long period events, volcanic tremors, and hybrid events, is used to train the models. Experimental analysis shows how neural activity and its associated specialization skills change depending on the architecture chosen and the type of event analyzed.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Inverse Abstraction of Neural Networks Using Symbolic Interpolation
papers.research_question: How to efficiently compute approximate representations (abstractions) of pre-image sets of neural networks, so that they are both compact and precise enough for enabling formal analysis, interpretation and knowledge/policy extraction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for computing symbolic abstractions of pre-images of neural networks using interpolation, enabling formal analysis and knowledge extraction without modifying the network.
papers.conclusion: The approach algorithmically abstracts neural network pre-images into compact representations that allow for interpretation and verification, opening directions for future work in verification and training.
papers.key_findings:
The method can compute compact overapproximations and underapproximations of pre-images for neural networks.
The extracted abstractions are interpretable and can be used for verifying properties (like robustness) and extracting control laws.
The method is demonstrated on control tasks (cart-pole and swimmer) and a 2D classification task.
The run-time scales exponentially with the number of nodes in a hidden layer and almost linearly with network depth.
The computed abstractions can be used to verify complex safety properties of neural network controllers.
papers.limitation:
The run-time scales exponentially with increasing number of nodes in a hidden layer.
The method is applicable to piecewise-linear neural networks.
future_direction: Coupling the approach with current verification algorithms to improve verification itself.
Coupling the abstraction procedure with training to learn neural networks that satisfy certain desired properties.
Tuning the abstraction to satisfy certain desired specifications without compromising significantly on performance.
papers.abstract: Neural networks in real-world applications have to satisfy critical properties such as safety and reliability. The analysis of such properties typically requires extracting information through computing pre-images of the network transformations, but it is well-known that explicit computation of pre-images is intractable. We introduce new methods for computing compact symbolic abstractions of pre-images by computing their overapproximations and underapproximations through all layers. The abstraction of pre-images enables formal analysis and knowledge extraction without affecting standard learning algorithms. We use inverse abstractions to automatically extract simple control laws and compact representations for pre-images corresponding to unsafe outputs. We illustrate that the extracted abstractions are interpretable and can be used for analyzing complex properties.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Sparse Autoencoder Features in Vision
papers.research_question: How to causally interpret sparse autoencoder features in vision transformers by identifying the image patches that drive activations, rather than relying on correlational activation maps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which uses effective receptive field attribution to provide causal explanations for SAE features in vision transformers, demonstrating improved faithfulness over activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: CaFE provides more faithful and semantically precise interpretations of visual features by using causal ERF-based explanations, preventing misinterpretation from activation-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
CaFE with ERF attribution more accurately identifies causal image patches for SAE feature activations compared to naive activation maps.
Non-localized SAE features exist, especially in higher layers, where activations scatter across the image.
ERF maps reveal hidden context dependencies, such as features requiring co-occurrence of multiple objects.
Insertion tests show that CaFE with AttnLRP achieves higher causal recovery rates than activation-based baselines.
The frequency of non-local features increases with transformer layer depth, peaking in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Computing the ERF for each feature requires both forward and backward passes, which may be costly for very deep SAEs.
Manual annotation of non-local features is inherently subjective; devising scalable, automated criteria remains future work.
future_direction: Devising scalable, automated criteria for identifying non-local features
Extending CaFE with ERF-based attribution to text modalities
papers.abstract: Understanding what sparse auto-encoder (SAE) features in vision transformers truly represent is usually done by inspecting the patches where a feature's activation is highest. However, self-attention mixes information across the entire image, so an activated patch often co-occurs with-but does not cause-the feature's firing. We propose Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which leverages Effective Receptive Field (ERF). We consider each activation of an SAE feature to be a target and apply input-attribution methods to identify the image patches that causally drive that activation. Across CLIP-ViT features, ERF maps frequently diverge from naive activation maps, revealing hidden context dependencies (e.g., a "roaring face" feature that requires the co-occurrence of eyes and nose, rather than merely an open mouth). Patch insertion tests confirm that CaFE more effectively recovers or suppresses feature activations than activation-ranked patches. Our results show that CaFE yields more faithful and semantically precise explanations of vision-SAE features, highlighting the risk of misinterpretation when relying solely on activation location.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: A Structured Dictionary Perspective on Implicit Neural Representations
papers.research_question: What is the expressive power of INRs? How does initialization affect their inductive bias?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a unified theoretical perspective on implicit neural representations (INRs), showing they are analogous to structured signal dictionaries with harmonics, and that their inductive bias is characterized by the neural tangent kernel (NTK), with meta-learning reshaping the NTK like dictionary learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes the expressive power and inductive bias of INRs from a unified perspective, showing harmonic expansion and NTK characterization, and reveals that meta-learning modifies the NTK to increase efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
INRs have expressive power equivalent to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the input mapping frequencies.
The frequency support of INRs grows exponentially with depth as each layer splits input into higher order harmonics.
INRs suffer from failure modes such as imperfect recovery and aliasing due to their harmonic expansion.
The inductive bias of INRs is captured by the ability of their empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) to encode target signals efficiently.
Meta-learning increases the encoding efficiency of the NTK by constructing a rich signal dictionary from combinations of meta-training tasks.
papers.limitation: Most practical results are performed using one or two-dimensional signals, and insights should be extensible to higher dimensions.
future_direction: Generalize Theorem 1 to input mappings beyond sinusoids or include normalization layers.
Study the effect of out-of-distribution data on the alignment with the NTK after meta-training.
Design methods to visualize the eigenfunctions of the NTK in higher dimensions.
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to classical discretized representations of signals. Nevertheless, despite their practical success, we still do not understand how INRs represent signals. We propose a novel unified perspective to theoretically analyse INRs. Leveraging results from harmonic analysis and deep learning theory, we show that most INR families are analogous to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the set of initial mapping frequencies. This structure allows INRs to express signals with an exponentially increasing frequency support using a number of parameters that only grows linearly with depth. We also explore the inductive bias of INRs exploiting recent results about the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK). Specifically, we show that the eigenfunctions of the NTK can be seen as dictionary atoms whose inner product with the target signal determines the final performance of their reconstruction. In this regard, we reveal that meta-learning has a reshaping effect on the NTK analogous to dictionary learning, building dictionary atoms as a combination of the examples seen during meta-training. Our results permit to design and tune novel INR architectures, but can also be of interest for the wider deep learning theory community.

papers.title: A Monosemantic Attribution Framework for Stable Interpretability in Clinical Neuroscience Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we produce stable, clinically meaningful explanations from large language models by integrating attributional and mechanistic interpretability to address polysemanticity and inter-method variability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction, using sparse autoencoders to transform polysemantic activations and an explanation optimizer (TEO) to produce stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed monosemantic attribution framework advances the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease by providing stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The SAE layer improves attribution stability (lower RIS/ROS) and clinical meaningfulness.
TEO with SAE (TEO-SAE) achieves the most stable attributions across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets.
The UMAP linear constraint helps linearize the attribution space and yields robust scores.
The framework provides clinically interpretable attribution maps highlighting relevant biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
SAE-guided attribution yields more reliable explanations than traditional attribution methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability remains a key challenge for deploying large language models (LLMs) in clinical settings such as Alzheimer's disease progression diagnosis, where early and trustworthy predictions are essential. Existing attribution methods exhibit high inter-method variability and unstable explanations due to the polysemantic nature of LLM representations, while mechanistic interpretability approaches lack direct alignment with model inputs and outputs and do not provide explicit importance scores. We introduce a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction. By constructing a monosemantic embedding space at the level of an LLM layer and optimizing the framework to explicitly reduce inter-method variability, our approach produces stable input-level importance scores and highlights salient features via a decompressed representation of the layer of interest, advancing the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
papers.research_question: How can saturation effects in gradient-based automated circuit identification methods be mitigated to improve attribution reliability and circuit faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EAP-GP, a gradient-based circuit identification method that uses a dynamically adjusted integration path (GradPath) to mitigate saturation effects, leading to more reliable edge attributions and more faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: EAP-GP effectively mitigates saturation effects in gradient-based circuit identification by using a dynamically adjusted integration path, leading to enhanced edge attribution accuracy and circuit faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-GP outperforms previous gradient-based methods (EAP and EAP-IG) in circuit faithfulness across six tasks, achieving improvements up to 17.7%.
EAP-GP maintains excellent performance on larger models (GPT-2 Medium and GPT-2 XL).
EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than existing methods when compared to manually annotated ground-truth circuits.
The method's performance is robust with only a few steps (k=4 or 5) in the GradPath construction.
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for path construction.
papers.limitation:
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for constructing the integration path.
Increasing the number of steps (k) in EAP-GP beyond an optimal point (e.g., k>5) can lead to performance degradation due to noise accumulation in the integration path near the corrupted input.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of transformer-based language models remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability based on circuit discovery aims to reverse engineer neural networks by analyzing their internal processes at the level of computational subgraphs. In this paper, we revisit existing gradient-based circuit identification methods and find that their performance is either affected by the zero-gradient problem or saturation effects, where edge attribution scores become insensitive to input changes, resulting in noisy and unreliable attribution evaluations for circuit components. To address the saturation effect, we propose Edge Attribution Patching with GradPath (EAP-GP), EAP-GP introduces an integration path, starting from the input and adaptively following the direction of the difference between the gradients of corrupted and clean inputs to avoid the saturated region. This approach enhances attribution reliability and improves the faithfulness of circuit identification. We evaluate EAP-GP on 6 datasets using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and GPT-2 XL. Experimental results demonstrate that EAP-GP outperforms existing methods in circuit faithfulness, achieving improvements up to 17.7%. Comparisons with manually annotated ground-truth circuits demonstrate that EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than previous approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying accurate circuits.

papers.title: Interpretable and Testable Vision Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we understand vision models by not only interpreting their learned features but also validating these interpretations through controlled experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a practical, post-hoc method that bridges the gap between concept discovery and causal probing in vision models, enabling both interpretation and controlled testing of learned features.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable both hypothesis formation and controlled testing for vision models, providing a foundation for empirically validated model interpretation that unites explanation with experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on vision transformer activations discover interpretable, monosemantic features corresponding to visual concepts (e.g., cultural symbols, abstract concepts like 'accidents').
CLIP, trained with language supervision, learns abstract semantic features (e.g., country-specific patterns, style-agnostic concepts) that DINOv2, trained with purely visual objectives, does not reliably capture.
SAE-derived features enable precise causal interventions: suppressing a 'blue feathers' feature in a bird image shifts the classification prediction to a similar bird without blue plumage.
SAE features behave as a pseudo-orthogonal basis; suppressing a concept like 'sand' in semantic segmentation affects only the targeted regions without meaningfully altering other predictions.
The method supports patch-level causal edits across different tasks (classification and segmentation) without retraining the original vision transformer or task heads.
papers.limitation:
Discovering interesting SAE units depends on manual browsing of exemplar grids, which is slow, may overlook concepts, and risks cherry-picking.
The work relies on qualitative evaluation through visual inspection, lacking standardized quantitative metrics for measuring interpretability and control effectiveness.
Large interventions on SAE features can push activations off-manifold, and feature correlations/complex interactions complicate clean causal attribution.
SAEs are not guaranteed to surface every concept a model encodes, and low-activation units can be polysemantic or vary across random initializations.
Validation is limited to fine-grained classification and semantic segmentation; broader task coverage and comparison to prior editable concept frameworks (e.g., DN-CBM) are needed.
future_direction: Automating feature discovery and concept-label assignment (e.g., via language supervision).
Developing robust quantitative metrics for semantic alignment, manipulation specificity, and cross-model comparability.
Extending reliable feature control to more sophisticated visual reasoning tasks and understanding feature interactions across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: To truly understand vision models, we must not only interpret their learned features but also validate these interpretations through controlled experiments. While earlier work offers either rich semantics or direct control, few post-hoc tools supply both in a single, model-agnostic procedure. We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to bridge this gap; each sparse feature comes with real-image exemplars that reveal its meaning and a decoding vector that can be manipulated to probe its influence on downstream task behavior. By applying our method to widely-used pre-trained vision models, we reveal meaningful differences in the semantic abstractions learned by different pre-training objectives. We then show that a single SAE trained on frozen ViT activations supports patch-level causal edits across tasks (classification and segmentation) all without retraining the ViT or task heads. These qualitative, falsifiable demonstrations position SAEs as a practical bridge between concept discovery and causal probing of vision models. We provide code, demos and models on our project website: https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/saev.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: Weights to Code: Extracting Interpretable Algorithms from the Discrete Transformer
papers.research_question: Is it possible to synthesize executable and interpretable programs by extracting algorithms from Transformer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Discrete Transformer, a transformer variant designed for algorithm extraction, and shows it can synthesize human-readable programs from weights via a modular pipeline combining hypothesis testing and symbolic regression.
papers.conclusion: The Discrete Transformer establishes a robust framework for demonstration-free algorithm discovery and Transformer interpretability, bridging continuous optimization and discrete symbolic logic.
papers.key_findings:
The Discrete Transformer achieves algorithm extraction performance comparable to RNN-based methods (MIPS) on a benchmark of algorithmic tasks.
It extracts exact algebraic expressions for non-linear tasks (e.g., parity as xt+xt-1-2*xt*xt-1).
It natively handles continuous-valued tasks, which prior discrete latent-state methods cannot.
Training dynamics exhibit a clear exploration-to-exploitation transition during temperature annealing.
Architectural inductive biases provide fine-grained control over the synthesized programs, enabling controllable algorithm discovery.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to tasks whose ground-truth mappings are representable under the symbolic regression tool's default operator set (e.g., +, -, *, /).
papers.abstract: Algorithm extraction aims to synthesize executable programs directly from models trained on specific algorithmic tasks, enabling de novo algorithm discovery without relying on human-written code. However, extending this paradigm to Transformer is hindered by superposition, where entangled features encoded in overlapping directions obstruct the extraction of symbolic expressions. In this work, we propose the Discrete Transformer, an architecture explicitly engineered to bridge the gap between continuous representations and discrete symbolic logic. By enforcing a strict functional disentanglement, which constrains Numerical Attention to information routing and Numerical MLP to element-wise arithmetic, and employing temperature-annealed sampling, our method effectively facilitates the extraction of human-readable programs. Empirically, the Discrete Transformer not only achieves performance comparable to RNN-based baselines but crucially extends interpretability to continuous variable domains. Moreover, our analysis of the annealing process shows that the efficient discrete search undergoes a clear phase transition from exploration to exploitation. We further demonstrate that our method enables fine-grained control over synthesized programs by imposing inductive biases. Collectively, these findings establish the Discrete Transformer as a robust framework for demonstration-free algorithm discovery, offering a rigorous pathway toward Transformer interpretability.

papers.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
papers.research_question: Why do neural networks arrive at particular computational strategies when trained on algebraic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that margin maximization can fully specify the features learned by neural networks on algebraic tasks, explaining why networks arrive at particular computational strategies such as Fourier features for modular addition.
papers.conclusion: Margin maximization fully specifies the features learned on algebraic tasks, providing insight into why networks adopt particular computational strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum margin solutions for modular addition use neurons that are sparse in Fourier space, each neuron corresponding to a single frequency.
For sparse parity, maximum margin solutions have neurons that assign equal magnitude weights to relevant bits and satisfy a sign condition.
For finite group operations, maximum margin solutions use neurons that correspond to irreducible representations of the group.
Neural networks trained with gradient descent and small regularization approach the maximum margin solution, and their learned features match the theoretical predictions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple architectures (one-hidden layer networks) and synthetic algebraic tasks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigate margin maximization in more realistic settings.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations learned by neural networks is a cornerstone challenge in the science of machine learning. While there have been significant recent strides in some cases towards understanding how neural networks implement specific target functions, this paper explores a complementary question -- why do networks arrive at particular computational strategies? Our inquiry focuses on the algebraic learning tasks of modular addition, sparse parities, and finite group operations. Our primary theoretical findings analytically characterize the features learned by stylized neural networks for these algebraic tasks. Notably, our main technique demonstrates how the principle of margin maximization alone can be used to fully specify the features learned by the network. Specifically, we prove that the trained networks utilize Fourier features to perform modular addition and employ features corresponding to irreducible group-theoretic representations to perform compositions in general groups, aligning closely with the empirical observations of Nanda et al. and Chughtai et al. More generally, we hope our techniques can help to foster a deeper understanding of why neural networks adopt specific computational strategies.

papers.title: NEWRON: A New Generalization of the Artificial Neuron to Enhance the Interpretability of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we design a novel neural network structure that makes the whole model interpretable without sacrificing effectiveness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NEWRON, a generalization of the artificial neuron that enables interpretable neural networks without losing expressive power, as proven by universal approximation theorems.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a generalized neuron concept with three specializations that retain the expressive power of standard neural networks while enabling interpretability, and experimental results show competitive performance with interpretable and non-interpretable models.
papers.key_findings:
NEWRON specializations allow interpretability by inspecting model parameters.
Universal approximation theorems hold for Heaviside, sigmoid, and tanh-prod IAN.
Experiments show NEWRON-based models outperform traditional interpretable models (decision trees, logistic regression) and perform similarly or better than standard neural networks on tabular data.
Heaviside IAN is the most interpretable but harder to train, while sigmoid and tanh-prod offer a trade-off.
The structure remains interpretable even with multiple layers.
papers.limitation:
The extraction of proper rules from the network can be harrowing; in the Heaviside case, they might be too long, and in the sigmoid and tanh-prod cases, their simplicity depends on the final parameter values.
The work has not compared NEWRON against state-of-the-art Deep Learning models for tabular data.
future_direction: Investigate the expressiveness of IAN-based models with respect to network depth and width.
Refine the analysis of the tanh-prod case as the number of tanh functions increases.
Extend the method to other neural models such as Recurrent, Convolutional, and Graph Neural Networks.
papers.abstract: In this work, we formulate NEWRON: a generalization of the McCulloch-Pitts neuron structure. This new framework aims to explore additional desirable properties of artificial neurons. We show that some specializations of NEWRON allow the network to be interpretable with no change in their expressiveness. By just inspecting the models produced by our NEWRON-based networks, we can understand the rules governing the task.
