Extensive experiments show that the quality of the generated models is better than traditional interpretable models and in line or better than standard neural networks.

papers.title: Formal Conceptual Views in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we provide global explanations for neural networks using a formal framework based on Formal Concept Analysis? Specifically, can conceptual views faithfully represent models, enable architecture comparison, and support abductive learning of human-comprehensible rules?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces conceptual views as a formal framework for global explanation of neural networks, enabling faithful representation, architecture comparison via Gromov-Wasserstein distance, and abductive learning of human-comprehensible rules from neurons.
papers.conclusion: Conceptual views offer a principled framework for the global analysis of neural networks, bridging neural and symbolic representations to improve explainability and enable symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Many-valued conceptual views achieve high fidelity as surrogates for the original neural network models.
The Gromov-Wasserstein distance applied to conceptual views yields meaningful similarity measures between different neural network architectures.
Symbolic conceptual views, particularly with Tanh activation, enable decision-tree based surrogates with competitive fidelity.
Background knowledge can be integrated via subgroup discovery to derive human-comprehensible rules about neurons.
The framework provides a principled bridge between neural representations and symbolic reasoning through Formal Concept Analysis.
papers.limitation:
Restriction to non-recursive architectures (feed-forward networks with a well-defined last hidden layer).
Requirement for multiple output neurons; effectiveness in regression settings is unexplored.
Dependence on domain-specific background knowledge for human-comprehensible explanations.
Threshold sensitivity: the quality of the symbolic view depends heavily on the activation function, with Tanh preferred over ReLU for dichotomic scaling.
Scalability: concept lattices grow exponentially with the number of attributes, limiting direct human inspection.
Scope of experiments is limited to image classification tasks; extension to other modalities and recent architectures is future work.
future_direction: Integrating the framework with concept bottleneck models to combine architectural and post-hoc interpretability.
Extending the symbolic view to intermediate layers for a multi-resolution analysis.
Exploring whether feedback from the symbolic analysis can guide model refinement, e.g., by identifying neurons that encode redundant or biased concepts.
papers.abstract: Explaining neural network models is a challenging task that remains unsolved in its entirety to this day. This is especially true for high dimensional and complex data. With the present work, we introduce two notions for conceptual views of a neural network, specifically a many-valued and a symbolic view. Both provide novel analysis methods to enable a human AI analyst to grasp deeper insights into the knowledge that is captured by the neurons of a network. We test the conceptual expressivity of our novel views through different experiments on the ImageNet and Fruit-360 data sets. Furthermore, we show to which extent the views allow to quantify the conceptual similarity of different learning architectures. Finally, we demonstrate how conceptual views can be applied for abductive learning of human comprehensible rules from neurons. In summary, with our work, we contribute to the most relevant task of globally explaining neural networks models.

papers.title: Granular Concept Circuits: Toward a Fine-Grained Circuit Discovery for Concept Representations
papers.research_question: How can we discover fine-grained circuits that represent specific visual concepts in deep image classification models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), a method for automatically discovering fine-grained circuits that represent specific visual concepts in deep image classification models.
papers.conclusion: Introduces Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), a novel method for fine-grained visual concept circuit discovery, contributing to AI interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
GCC can discover multiple distinct concept circuits for a single query, enabling fine-grained interpretation.
GCC is effective across various model architectures (CNNs and Transformers) and datasets.
Ablation of neurons in GCC leads to significant logit/accuracy drops, demonstrating faithfulness and completeness.
User study shows that GCC circuits are perceived as meaningful and diverse by human evaluators.
GCC can be applied to audit misclassifications and identify shared concepts across different classes.
papers.limitation:
Connectivity is evaluated in a model-centric manner, so some strongly associated connections may remain difficult to interpret.
A single concept may be distributed across multiple circuit pathways, especially under strict connectivity thresholds.
papers.abstract: Deep vision models have achieved remarkable classification performance by leveraging a hierarchical architecture in which human-interpretable concepts emerge through the composition of individual neurons across layers. Given the distributed nature of representations, pinpointing where specific visual concepts are encoded within a model remains a crucial yet challenging task. In this paper, we introduce an effective circuit discovery method, called Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), in which each circuit represents a concept relevant to a given query. To construct each circuit, our method iteratively assesses inter-neuron connectivity, focusing on both functional dependencies and semantic alignment. By automatically discovering multiple circuits, each capturing specific concepts within that query, our approach offers a profound, concept-wise interpretation of models and is the first to identify circuits tied to specific visual concepts at a fine-grained level. We validate the versatility and effectiveness of GCCs across various deep image classification models.

papers.title: Feature Accentuation: Revealing 'What' Features Respond to in Natural Images
papers.research_question: How can we understand both where and what in natural images induces a feature's response in neural network vision models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Accentuation, an image-seeded feature visualization method that generates naturalistic visual explanations for features in images, revealing both where and what the feature responds to, and validates that these accentuations are processed along natural circuits.
papers.conclusion: Feature Accentuation is a useful tool for interpretability that provides meaningful and natural explanations by exaggerating features in images, aiding in understanding model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Feature accentuation can generate high-quality visual counterfactual explanations for non-robust models without auxiliary generative models.
The accentuations follow natural circuits in the model, showing higher path similarity to natural images than natural images themselves (super-natural).
Feature accentuation helps in understanding model misclassifications by exaggerating the predicted logit, allowing humans to see the same hallucination.
In a human experiment, feature accentuation explanations yield better extrapolation than dataset examples for atypical feature activations.
papers.limitation:
Creating realistic images does not automatically guarantee effective explanations of neural networks.
Feature visualizations might need to produce images that deviate from the original input, potentially conflicting with the proposed regularization.
Feature visualizations have limited interpretability for humans, and dataset examples can be more effective; thus supplementary tools are needed.
papers.abstract: Efforts to decode neural network vision models necessitate a comprehensive grasp of both the spatial and semantic facets governing feature responses within images. Most research has primarily centered around attribution methods, which provide explanations in the form of heatmaps, showing where the model directs its attention for a given feature. However, grasping 'where' alone falls short, as numerous studies have highlighted the limitations of those methods and the necessity to understand 'what' the model has recognized at the focal point of its attention. In parallel, 'Feature visualization' offers another avenue for interpreting neural network features. This approach synthesizes an optimal image through gradient ascent, providing clearer insights into 'what' features respond to. However, feature visualizations only provide one global explanation per feature; they do not explain why features activate for particular images. In this work, we introduce a new method to the interpretability tool-kit, 'feature accentuation', which is capable of conveying both where and what in arbitrary input images induces a feature's response. At its core, feature accentuation is image-seeded (rather than noise-seeded) feature visualization. We find a particular combination of parameterization, augmentation, and regularization yields naturalistic visualizations that resemble the seed image and target feature simultaneously. Furthermore, we validate these accentuations are processed along a natural circuit by the model. We make our precise implementation of feature accentuation available to the community as the Faccent library, an extension of Lucent.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: NIMO: a Nonlinear Interpretable MOdel
papers.research_question: How can we combine the inherent interpretability of linear models (via clear feature effects) with the expressive power of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NIMO, a hybrid model that preserves the global interpretability of linear coefficients (marginal effects at the mean) while adding per-instance nonlinear corrections via a neural network, along with an efficient optimization method based on parameter elimination.
papers.conclusion: NIMO provides a promising framework for interpretable machine learning, successfully combining the intelligibility of linear models with the flexibility of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
NIMO outperforms baseline methods (Lasso, NN, NAM, IMN, LassoNet) on synthetic datasets and remains robust in low-data regimes.
NIMO accurately recovers the true linear coefficients (marginal effects at the mean) and sparsity patterns on synthetic data, preserving global interpretability.
On real-world datasets (Diabetes, Boston Housing, Superconductivity), NIMO achieves predictive performance comparable to or better than other methods while providing interpretable coefficients.
The model's architecture (masking the j-th feature input to its correction network) is crucial for preserving the interpretation of the linear coefficients.
NIMO cannot capture self-nonlinearities (e.g., x^2) in the raw feature space without explicit basis expansion, which is a known limitation.
papers.limitation: NIMO cannot capture self-nonlinearities (e.g., x_j^2) in the raw feature space due to its interpretability-preserving architecture; such effects require explicit basis expansion.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has achieved remarkable success across many domains, but it has also created a growing demand for interpretability in model predictions. Although many explainable machine learning methods have been proposed, post-hoc explanations lack guaranteed fidelity and are sensitive to hyperparameter choices, highlighting the appeal of inherently interpretable models. For example, linear regression provides clear feature effects through its coefficients. However, such models are often outperformed by more complex neural networks (NNs) that usually lack inherent interpretability. To address this dilemma, we introduce NIMO, a framework that combines inherent interpretability with the expressive power of neural networks. Building on the simple linear regression, NIMO is able to provide flexible and intelligible feature effects. Relevantly, we develop an optimization method based on parameter elimination, that allows for optimizing the NN parameters and linear coefficients effectively and efficiently. By relying on adaptive ridge regression we can easily incorporate sparsity as well. We show empirically that our model can provide faithful and intelligible feature effects while maintaining good predictive performance.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Successor Heads: Recurring, Interpretable Attention Heads In The Wild
papers.research_question: Do recurring, interpretable attention heads (successor heads) exist in large language models, and how do they work?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces successor heads, a class of attention heads that increment tokens in ordinal sequences, and finds that they use abstract mod-10 features across model architectures and scales.
papers.conclusion: Successor heads are a recurring, interpretable component in LLMs that use compositional mod-10 features for incrementation, providing insights into numeric representations and model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Successor heads exist across models from 31M to 12B parameters and across architectures (GPT-2, Pythia, Llama-2).
Successor heads use compositional numeric representations with mod-10 features.
Vector arithmetic with mod-10 features can steer head behavior.
Successor heads are important for low loss on incrementation tasks in natural language data.
Successor heads exhibit polysemanticity (also perform acronym prediction).
papers.limitation:
Mod-10 features do not fully capture the greater-than bias and fail to steer Days and Letters tasks.
The numeric projection might capture more than just the numeric subspace, affecting successor decoding.
future_direction: Future work on how language models represent numeric concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work we present successor heads: attention heads that increment tokens with a natural ordering, such as numbers, months, and days. For example, successor heads increment 'Monday' into 'Tuesday'. We explain the successor head behavior with an approach rooted in mechanistic interpretability, the field that aims to explain how models complete tasks in human-understandable terms. Existing research in this area has found interpretable language model components in small toy models. However, results in toy models have not yet led to insights that explain the internals of frontier models and little is currently understood about the internal operations of large language models. In this paper, we analyze the behavior of successor heads in large language models (LLMs) and find that they implement abstract representations that are common to different architectures. They form in LLMs with as few as 31 million parameters, and at least as many as 12 billion parameters, such as GPT-2, Pythia, and Llama-2. We find a set of 'mod-10 features' that underlie how successor heads increment in LLMs across different architectures and sizes. We perform vector arithmetic with these features to edit head behavior and provide insights into numeric representations within LLMs. Additionally, we study the behavior of successor heads on natural language data, identifying interpretable polysemanticity in a Pythia successor head.

papers.title: The Features at Convergence Theorem: a first-principles alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz for how networks learn representations
papers.research_question: Is there an alternative to the empirically-observed Neural Feature Ansatz conjecture, which can be derived from first principles?
papers.core_contribution: Derives the Features at Convergence Theorem (FACT) from first-order optimality conditions, providing a principled alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) that holds at convergence and captures feature learning phenomena.
papers.conclusion: FACT provides a first-principles alternative to the NFA, unifying theoretical optimality conditions with empirical feature learning, and captures global behaviors like grokking and phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
FACT, derived from first-order optimality, must hold at convergence and shows higher correlation with learned features than NFA and eNFA.
FACT captures feature learning phenomena such as grokking in modular arithmetic and phase transitions in sparse parity learning, similar to NFA.
FACT explains why NFA usually holds, as the two are proportional in many settings (e.g., modular arithmetic).
In degenerate settings, NFA can be nearly uncorrelated with the learned features while FACT still holds.
FACT-RFM achieves comparable performance to NFA-RFM on tabular data and synthetic tasks.
papers.limitation:
FACT has low correlation with neural feature matrices during most of training prior to interpolation, limiting its use for understanding feature evolution during training.
FACT requires non-zero weight decay, and it is unclear how to compute it in the zero weight-decay limit.
FACT-RFM can become unstable if continued iterations are performed after convergence, requiring early stopping in some settings.
future_direction: Derive a quantity with more stable correlation over training.
Understand the instability of FACT-RFM after convergence.
Compute FACT without weight decay via the neural tangent kernel.
papers.abstract: It is a central challenge in deep learning to understand how neural networks learn representations. A leading approach is the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) (Radhakrishnan et al. 2024), a conjectured mechanism for how feature learning occurs. Although the NFA is empirically validated, it is an educated guess and lacks a theoretical basis, and thus it is unclear when it might fail, and how to improve it. In this paper, we take a first-principles approach to understanding why this observation holds, and when it does not. We use first-order optimality conditions to derive the Features at Convergence Theorem (FACT), an alternative to the NFA that (a) obtains greater agreement with learned features at convergence, (b) explains why the NFA holds in most settings, and (c) captures essential feature learning phenomena in neural networks such as grokking behavior in modular arithmetic and phase transitions in learning sparse parities, similarly to the NFA. Thus, our results unify theoretical first-order optimality analyses of neural networks with the empirically-driven NFA literature, and provide a principled alternative that provably and empirically holds at convergence.

papers.title: Emergent Symbol-like Number Variables in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and how can we interpret neural network solutions through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: We extend the Distributed Alignment Search framework with alignment functions to interpret neural network activity in terms of symbolic variables, and show that recurrent networks develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the utility of causal interpretability tools and alignment functions for understanding neural representations, showing that RNNs develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent models (GRUs/LSTMs) develop graded symbol-like number variables within their neural activity.
Seemingly insignificant task variations can drastically affect alignment to Symbolic Algorithms, motivating extended DAS with alignment functions (LAFs).
Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) can control NN behavior through neural activity aligned to interpretable Symbolic Algorithms.
Shallow Transformers use anti-Markovian solutions to numeric tasks, and theoretically, Transformers must use anti-Markovian solutions without sufficient attention layers.
Causal interventions on neural subspaces are useful for NN interpretability.
papers.abstract: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and what would a satisfying answer to this question look like? In this work, we interpret Neural Network (NN) solutions to sequence based number tasks using a variety of methods to understand how well we can interpret them through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms (SAs) -- precise programs describable by rules and typed, mutable variables. We use autoregressive GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformers trained on tasks where the correct tokens depend on numeric information only latent in the task structure. We show through multiple causal and theoretical methods that we can interpret raw NN activity through the lens of simplified SAs when we frame the activity in terms of neural subspaces rather than individual neurons. Using Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), we find that, depending on network architecture, dimensionality, and task specifications, alignments with SA's can be very high, or they can be only approximate, or fail altogether. We extend our analytic toolkit to address the failure cases by expanding the DAS framework to a broader class of alignment functions that more flexibly capture NN activity in terms of interpretable variables from SAs, and we provide theoretic and empirical explorations of Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) in contrast to the preexisting Orthogonal Alignment Functions (OAFs). Through analyses of specific cases we confirm the usefulness of causal interventions on neural subspaces for NN interpretability, and we show that recurrent models can develop graded, symbol-like number variables in their neural activity. We further show that shallow Transformers learn very different solutions than recurrent networks, and we prove that such models must use anti-Markovian solutions -- solutions that do not rely on cumulative, Markovian hidden states -- in the absence of sufficient attention layers.

papers.title: Explaining Explanations: Axiomatic Feature Interactions for Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explain pairwise feature interactions in neural networks in a way that satisfies common-sense axioms and is applicable to any architecture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Hessians, an extension of Integrated Gradients that explains pairwise feature interactions in neural networks, satisfies proposed axioms, works on any architecture, and outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: Integrated Hessians is a theoretically grounded and empirically effective method for explaining pairwise feature interactions in neural networks, applicable to any differentiable model and providing insights in various domains.
papers.key_findings:
Integrated Hessians satisfies interaction completeness, self-completeness, and other axioms for feature interactions.
The method can be applied to ReLU networks by smoothing with SoftPlus, and requires fewer gradient calls for approximation.
Integrated Hessians outperforms existing methods (Shapley Interaction Index, Contextual Decomposition, etc.) in identifying interactions in synthetic data benchmarks.
The method is computationally efficient for models with many features, scaling better than existing methods.
In NLP, Integrated Hessians reveals intuitive interactions like negation patterns, and in drug response prediction, it identifies biologically plausible drug-drug interactions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown great promise in explaining neural network behavior. In particular, feature attribution methods explain which features were most important to a model's prediction on a given input. However, for many tasks, simply knowing which features were important to a model's prediction may not provide enough insight to understand model behavior. The interactions between features within the model may better help us understand not only the model, but also why certain features are more important than others. In this work, we present Integrated Hessians, an extension of Integrated Gradients that explains pairwise feature interactions in neural networks. Integrated Hessians overcomes several theoretical limitations of previous methods to explain interactions, and unlike such previous methods is not limited to a specific architecture or class of neural network. Additionally, we find that our method is faster than existing methods when the number of features is large, and outperforms previous methods on existing quantitative benchmarks. Code available at https://github.com/suinleelab/path_explain

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: $\textit{Revelio}$: Interpreting and leveraging semantic information in diffusion models
papers.research_question: What flavors of visual information are captured in different layers and timesteps of a diffusion model? How do they interact and complement each other? What inductive biases are captured in convolution-based vs transformer-based diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Revelio, a method using k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE) to uncover monosemantic interpretable features in diffusion models, and demonstrates the effectiveness of diffusion features for transfer learning via a lightweight classifier (Diff-C).
papers.key_findings:
Representation granularity varies non-linearly with model depth, with different layers capturing varying levels of visual semantics.
Representation granularity and generalizability vary with diffusion architectures, pre-training data, and design choices like latent vs pixel space.
k-sparse autoencoders help isolate monosemantic visual properties across model states, aiding interpretation.
Diffusion features are effective for discriminative tasks and visual reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight classifier.
Different diffusion timesteps capture different information granularities, with earlier timesteps better for fine-grained tasks.
future_direction: Deeper investigation into why additional noise at certain timesteps (e.g., t=200) helps feature generalizability.
Further research to understand why SD 1.5 performs better than SD 2.1 across timesteps, as noted in prior zero-shot classification work.
papers.abstract: We study $\textit{how}$ rich visual semantic information is represented within various layers and denoising timesteps of different diffusion architectures. We uncover monosemantic interpretable features by leveraging k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE). We substantiate our mechanistic interpretations via transfer learning using light-weight classifiers on off-the-shelf diffusion models' features. On $4$ datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of diffusion features for representation learning. We provide an in-depth analysis of how different diffusion architectures, pre-training datasets, and language model conditioning impacts visual representation granularity, inductive biases, and transfer learning capabilities. Our work is a critical step towards deepening interpretability of black-box diffusion models. Code and visualizations available at: https://github.com/revelio-diffusion/revelio

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Interpretability Evals for Dictionary Learning Interpretability Evals Case Study Self-explaining SAE features
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs.
papers.conclusion: New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Eval and Sort eval provide measures of SAE feature interpretability that correlate with evaluation loss.
Non-vanilla SAE variants (TopK, Gated, Tanh, JumpReLU) perform better than vanilla SAEs on interpretability evals.
The self-explaining method via feature injection works well for early layer features but is less effective for complex concepts and larger models.
Interpretability evals can derisk the adoption of new SAE methods by providing quality metrics.
The evaluations are not comprehensive and measure only a single notion of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The evals are not comprehensive and only measure a single notion of interpretability, which is nebulous.
The evaluations likely do not have the resolution to distinguish small performance differences between SAE variants.
The self-explaining method succeeds less often on larger models and is sensitive to scale.
future_direction: Creating more and better evaluations for sparse autoencoders.
Using self-explaining techniques as complementary tools in interpretability.
papers.abstract: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability? Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs. New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.

papers.title: HOPE: High-order Polynomial Expansion of Black-box Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we accurately and efficiently approximate a black-box neural network with an explicit, interpretable high-order Taylor polynomial?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HOPE, a method to expand a neural network into a high-order Taylor polynomial on a reference input, providing an accurate, efficient, and interpretable local approximation of the black-box model.
papers.conclusion: HOPE provides a high-precision polynomial interpretation of black-box neural networks, making them more transparent and applicable, with advantages in accuracy, computational cost, and convergence.
papers.key_findings:
HOPE computes high-order derivatives more accurately and efficiently than computational-graph-based methods like Autograd.
The Taylor polynomial provides a high-fidelity local approximation of the neural network's input-output mapping.
The convergence of the Taylor series depends on the parameter distribution of the network (weights near zero promote convergence).
HOPE enables applications such as function discovery, fast inference, and feature selection.
The method provides theoretical upper and lower bounds for the approximation error between the network and its Taylor polynomial.
papers.limitation: HOPE can only be applied to modules that are n-order differentiable; for networks with components like ReLU or Max Pooling, only first-order derivatives can be obtained.
future_direction: Explore the relationship between Taylor series convergence and parameter distribution to guide network optimization and design.
Investigate the use of high-order heat maps for more accurate input contribution analysis.
Leverage HOPE's ability to compute derivatives between any network nodes to inspire lightweight network design.
papers.abstract: Despite their remarkable performance, deep neural networks remain mostly ``black boxes'', suggesting inexplicability and hindering their wide applications in fields requiring making rational decisions. Here we introduce HOPE (High-order Polynomial Expansion), a method for expanding a network into a high-order Taylor polynomial on a reference input. Specifically, we derive the high-order derivative rule for composite functions and extend the rule to neural networks to obtain their high-order derivatives quickly and accurately. From these derivatives, we can then derive the Taylor polynomial of the neural network, which provides an explicit expression of the network's local interpretations. Numerical analysis confirms the high accuracy, low computational complexity, and good convergence of the proposed method. Moreover, we demonstrate HOPE's wide applications built on deep learning, including function discovery, fast inference, and feature selection. The code is available at https://github.com/HarryPotterXTX/HOPE.git.

papers.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the instability of existing Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for concept extraction and proposes a method to improve stability while maintaining reconstruction quality.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Archetypal SAEs, which constrain dictionary atoms to the convex hull of data, significantly improving stability while matching state-of-the-art reconstruction abilities.
papers.conclusion: Archetypal SAEs provide a stable and effective framework for concept extraction in large vision models, addressing a critical limitation of current SAE methods and advancing interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs exhibit severe instability across training runs, undermining their reliability as an interpretability tool.
Archetypal SAEs (A-SAEs) and their relaxed variants (RA-SAEs) achieve much higher stability without compromising reconstruction fidelity.
RA-SAEs outperform standard SAEs and classical dictionary learning methods on stability-reconstruction tradeoff.
The proposed methods uncover novel, semantically meaningful concepts in large-scale vision models.
Two new benchmarks (plausibility and identifiability) show that A-SAEs recover true classification directions and disentangle synthetic concept mixtures more effectively.
papers.limitation: The exact convex hull of the data is intractable to compute for large datasets, requiring a distillation step (e.g., K-Means) to obtain a subset of points.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful framework for machine learning interpretability, enabling the unsupervised decomposition of model representations into a dictionary of abstract, human-interpretable concepts. However, we reveal a fundamental limitation: existing SAEs exhibit severe instability, as identical models trained on similar datasets can produce sharply different dictionaries, undermining their reliability as an interpretability tool. To address this issue, we draw inspiration from the Archetypal Analysis framework introduced by Cutler & Breiman (1994) and present Archetypal SAEs (A-SAE), wherein dictionary atoms are constrained to the convex hull of data. This geometric anchoring significantly enhances the stability of inferred dictionaries, and their mildly relaxed variants RA-SAEs further match state-of-the-art reconstruction abilities. To rigorously assess dictionary quality learned by SAEs, we introduce two new benchmarks that test (i) plausibility, if dictionaries recover "true" classification directions and (ii) identifiability, if dictionaries disentangle synthetic concept mixtures. Across all evaluations, RA-SAEs consistently yield more structured representations while uncovering novel, semantically meaningful concepts in large-scale vision models.

papers.title: Neural Feature Learning in Function Space
papers.research_question: How can we learn feature representations that capture the statistical dependence of data and be assembled to build different inference models without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for learning feature representations that capture statistical dependence, using a function-space geometry (feature geometry) and a nesting technique, enabling the learned features to be assembled for various inference tasks without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework for neural feature learning in function space, connecting statistical dependence with feature representations and providing a systematic approach to learning algorithm design for various inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The feature geometry connects statistical dependence with feature spaces, allowing dependence to be represented and approximated by operations in feature spaces.
The nesting technique provides a systematic way to design learning algorithms for optimal feature extraction using standard neural network architectures and optimizers.
The framework is applied to multivariate learning problems, including conditional inference and multimodal learning with missing modalities, revealing connections to classical approaches like maximum likelihood estimation.
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework for learning system design with neural feature extractors. First, we introduce the feature geometry, which unifies statistical dependence and feature representations in a function space equipped with inner products. This connection defines function-space concepts on statistical dependence, such as norms, orthogonal projection, and spectral decomposition, exhibiting clear operational meanings. In particular, we associate each learning setting with a dependence component and formulate learning tasks as finding corresponding feature approximations. We propose a nesting technique, which provides systematic algorithm designs for learning the optimal features from data samples with off-the-shelf network architectures and optimizers. We further demonstrate multivariate learning applications, including conditional inference and multimodal learning, where we present the optimal features and reveal their connections to classical approaches.

papers.title: Training neural networks to encode symbols enables combinatorial generalization
papers.research_question: Can neural networks achieve combinatorial generalization when trained to explicitly represent symbols?
papers.core_contribution: Training neural networks to output explicit symbolic representations (VARS) enables combinatorial generalization in both symbolic and non-symbolic outputs.
papers.conclusion: Conventional neural networks can support combinatorial generalization when trained to explicitly represent symbols, challenging the view that dedicated symbolic mechanisms are necessary.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained with VARS achieve combinatorial generalization in a short-term memory task (Simulation 1).
Neural networks trained with VARS achieve combinatorial generalization in a visual reasoning task (Simulation 2).
The same networks without VARS training fail or perform poorly in combinatorial generalization.
The VARS method allows representing symbolic structures as fixed-size vectors that can be learned by standard neural networks.
The pressure to output symbolic representations changes the internal representations of the network, enabling better generalization.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear whether mainstream connectionism can address all concerns about combinatorial generalization, and there may be other cases that cannot be accounted for by purely connectionist models even with symbolic pressure.
More sophisticated symbolic thought, such as language and analogy-making, remains a challenge for sub-symbolic approaches.
future_direction: More research on pushing the boundaries of neural networks without dedicated symbolic mechanisms.
Investigating what kind of models provide the best account of human learning and performance.
papers.abstract: Combinatorial generalization-the ability to understand and produce novel combinations of already familiar elements-is considered to be a core capacity of the human mind and a major challenge to neural network models. A significant body of research suggests that conventional neural networks cannot solve this problem unless they are endowed with mechanisms specifically engineered for the purpose of representing symbols. In this paper, we introduce a novel way of representing symbolic structures in connectionist terms-the vectors approach to representing symbols (VARS), which allows training standard neural architectures to encode symbolic knowledge explicitly at their output layers. In two simulations, we show that neural networks not only can learn to produce VARS representations, but in doing so they achieve combinatorial generalization in their symbolic and non-symbolic output. This adds to other recent work that has shown improved combinatorial generalization under some training conditions, and raises the question of whether specific mechanisms or training routines are needed to support symbolic processing. This article is part of the theme issue 'Towards mechanistic models of meaning composition'.

papers.title: Node-By-Node Greedy Deep Learning for Interpretable Features
papers.research_question: Can a greedy node-by-node training algorithm for deep networks achieve comparable performance to standard layer-by-layer methods while being faster and producing more interpretable internal features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a greedy node-by-node training algorithm for deep networks that is orders of magnitude faster and produces more interpretable node-level features while maintaining comparable out-of-sample performance to standard layer-by-layer methods.
papers.conclusion: The greedy node-by-node deep learning algorithms (GN and GCN) achieve prediction performance comparable to standard layer-by-layer methods while offering significant speedup and more interpretable features.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed greedy node-by-node algorithm is orders of magnitude faster than standard layer-by-layer pre-training.
The features learned by the proposed algorithm are more interpretable (e.g., visually recognizable digit patterns) compared to those from layer-by-layer training.
The classification performance of the proposed algorithm is comparable to standard layer-by-layer methods across multiple datasets.
The amnesia factor is crucial for coordinating feature learning and avoiding redundant features, with an optimal value around 0.4-0.5.
The algorithm distributes data among nodes to learn distinct features, mimicking a human-like sequential feature learning process.
papers.limitation:
The algorithm learns features sequentially and is not easily parallelizable, posing scalability challenges for modern parallel computing architectures.
The paper does not investigate optimal hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, amnesia factor) for each inner node or layer, which may affect performance.
future_direction: Investigate better ways to partition the data among nodes.
Determine the optimal amnesia factor and learning rate for each node or layer.
Adapt the algorithm to parallel computing architectures, potentially by learning several features simultaneously on different machines and exchanging information.
papers.abstract: Multilayer networks have seen a resurgence under the umbrella of deep learning. Current deep learning algorithms train the layers of the network sequentially, improving algorithmic performance as well as providing some regularization. We present a new training algorithm for deep networks which trains \emph{each node in the network} sequentially. Our algorithm is orders of magnitude faster, creates more interpretable internal representations at the node level, while not sacrificing on the ultimate out-of-sample performance.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: What multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve tasks?
papers.core_contribution: We propose the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF) to trace and analyze the thought processes of language models during complex reasoning tasks by combining circuit analysis and self-influence functions.
papers.conclusion: The SICAF framework successfully maps hierarchical reasoning pathways in GPT-2 for the IOI task, revealing a human-like reasoning structure and enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace and analyze the thought processes of LMs in complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified for the IOI task are small (1-2% of edges) and faithful (recover ≥85% of model performance).
EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL outperform EAP in normalized faithfulness and converge with fewer parameters.
The model's key parameters for the IOI task are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The model follows a hierarchical reasoning path: identifying entities in early layers, interpreting actions in middle layers, and synthesizing information in final layers.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
The work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of the approach across varied tasks and model architectures.
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency of self-influence calculation.

papers.title: Cross-Attention Head Position Patterns Can Align with Human Visual Concepts in Text-to-Image Generative Models
papers.research_question: Can cross-attention heads in text-to-image diffusion models be aligned with human visual concepts, and how can this alignment be used to improve visual generative tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Head Relevance Vectors (HRVs) that align cross-attention heads with human visual concepts, and demonstrates that HRVs can be used as interpretable features to improve image generation, editing, and multi-concept generation.
papers.conclusion: HRVs provide an advancement in understanding cross-attention layers in text-to-image diffusion models and introduce new approaches for fine-grained control at the head level.
papers.key_findings:
HRVs serve as interpretable features, as shown by ordered weakening analysis where weakening heads in order of relevance removes the corresponding visual concept faster.
Applying HRVs via concept adjusting reduces misinterpretation of polysemous words in image generation from 63.0% to 15.9%.
Incorporating HRVs into P2P (concept strengthening) improves image editing for challenging attributes (color, material, geometric patterns, image style, weather conditions), achieving higher CLIP scores and human preference.
Incorporating HRVs into Attend-and-Excite (concept strengthening) reduces catastrophic neglect in multi-concept generation, improving performance by 2.3% to 6.3% across benchmarks.
HRVs are consistent across different models (Stable Diffusion v1.4 and SDXL) and allow flexible addition of new visual concepts.
papers.limitation:
The underlying T2I model may struggle to correctly understand certain concepts (e.g., Counting, Lighting Conditions), making it difficult to assess HRV relevance.
HRVs may fail to identify meaningful head orderings for some concepts (e.g., Facial Expression), possibly due to overly broad concept-words.
For SDXL, the normalization of HRV vectors (L1 norm equal to H=1300) may cause some elements to become too large when rescaling, potentially affecting generation quality.
future_direction: Explore normalization strategies for HRV vectors in models with many heads (e.g., clamping elements to an upper bound).
Address failure cases with more advanced T2I models in the future.
Further investigate the limitation with Facial Expression and refine concept-words.
papers.abstract: Recent text-to-image diffusion models leverage cross-attention layers, which have been effectively utilized to enhance a range of visual generative tasks. However, our understanding of cross-attention layers remains somewhat limited. In this study, we introduce a mechanistic interpretability approach for diffusion models by constructing Head Relevance Vectors (HRVs) that align with human-specified visual concepts. An HRV for a given visual concept has a length equal to the total number of cross-attention heads, with each element representing the importance of the corresponding head for the given visual concept. To validate HRVs as interpretable features, we develop an ordered weakening analysis that demonstrates their effectiveness. Furthermore, we propose concept strengthening and concept adjusting methods and apply them to enhance three visual generative tasks. Our results show that HRVs can reduce misinterpretations of polysemous words in image generation, successfully modify five challenging attributes in image editing, and mitigate catastrophic neglect in multi-concept generation. Overall, our work provides an advancement in understanding cross-attention layers and introduces new approaches for fine-controlling these layers at the head level.

papers.title: Supervised sparse auto-encoders as unconstrained feature models for semantic composition
papers.research_question: How can we address the limitations of unsupervised sparse auto-encoders (non-smooth L1 penalty and lack of semantic alignment) by using a supervised, decoder-only framework based on unconstrained feature models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised sparse auto-encoder (SSAE) framework that uses predefined sparse concept structure and decoder-only training to avoid L1 penalties and guarantee semantic alignment, enabling compositional generalization and feature-level editing.
papers.conclusion: The SSAE framework offers a scalable approach for interpretable control in large foundation models, providing an alternative to unsupervised SAEs for applications requiring feature-level modularity, editability, and semantic alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SSAE framework supports compositional generalization, successfully reconstructing images with concept combinations unseen during training.
The method enables feature-level intervention for semantic image editing without modifying the original prompt text.
The framework is simple, task- and model-agnostic, and can be applied to hidden activations in transformers, U-Net layers, or other hidden representations in foundation models.
The method avoids the optimization challenges of L1 regularization and the need for a trained encoder by design.
The approach is validated on Stable Diffusion 3.5, demonstrating the ability to isolate and manipulate concepts like hair color and object presence.
papers.limitation:
The model can only edit concepts that were included in the supervised dictionary and does not support discovery of new, emergent features.
Building high-quality concept dictionaries requires human input and may not scale easily to thousands of attributes.
Due to computational constraints, the experiments are not large-scale and do not include training an encoder, limiting the assessment of the method's full potential and performance on inputs unrelated to training examples.
The method was only tested on prompt embeddings from Stable Diffusion 3.5, and its generality across other models and domains (e.g., text generation, video generation) is not yet assessed.
future_direction: Automating concept dictionary construction using large (vision) language models.
Scaling up experiments (more prompts, higher concept subspace dimension) to reach full potential and benchmark against state-of-the-art editing methods.
Applying the same architecture to U-Net feature maps or transformer hidden states to assess generality across application domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) have re-emerged as a prominent method for mechanistic interpretability, yet they face two significant challenges: the non-smoothness of the $L_1$ penalty, which hinders reconstruction and scalability, and a lack of alignment between learned features and human semantics.
